speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, January 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Stevens that Bill C-15, an Act respecting investment in Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Regional Development; and on the motion of Mrs. Tardif (Charlesbourg) (p. 1708).
Is the House ready for the question?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising to oppose the motion that was moved yesterday by the Government. The motion in question is intended to choke off debate at a most inappropriate time. Certainly when we are dealing with a measure of the importance claimed for the Bill to create Investment Canada, by the Government, I would submit that the measure would require the widest and deepest possible consideration, not only in committee but in the formal stages of debate here in the House.
Instead of allowing this debate to continue, instead of allowing Members of the House to have the fullest opportunity to express their views and concerns during the second reading stage, the Government has moved an amendment to have the previous question put, thereby shutting off the opportunity that would otherwise exist for Members of the House to offer reasoned amendments and to bring about a vote on second reading. I submit that this is most inappropriate and most untimely. This motion deserves to be rejected by the House.
Aside from the reason I have already stated, that the motion is designed to choke off debate on second reading before Members of the House feel they have had adequate time to express their views at this stage, another reason to oppose this motion is that the Bill itself has not been shown to be one worthy of the support of the House. The debate that has gone on over the past several weeks, rather than strengthening the case made for the Bill by the Government, has, in my view, done just the opposite.
In proposing to Parliament the Bill to create Investment Canada, the Government has given as a reason for it the notion that the creation of Investment Canada would in itself
cause a massive flow into Canada of the kind of investment needed to create jobs and bring about economic growth. However, it is most interesting to note that after the Bill was presented to the House for second reading, a number of articles appeared in the press examining this very question. The articles all came to the conclusion that the Bill itself would not really do anything to bring to Canada the kind of investment we continue to need in order to create jobs and generally improve the economy.
The articles in question pointed out, as I did in an earlier speech in the House, that what brings investment to a country or community is the view of the potential investor that there are profits to be made and that there are markets to be filled. In other words, investment is brought to a community when there are demands for the products or services intended to be created by the investment, demands sufficient that these products or services can be sold at a profit. The Investment Canada Bill does nothing whatsoever to improve the prospects for investors of making a profit through investing in Canada, whether they are foreign or Canadian investors. This Bill does nothing to improve the conditions in the Canadian economy which would lead investors to believe that they have a reasonable chance to make a profit beyond the situation existing at present.
Let me outline some of these factors and try to relate them to the Bill. One of the factors is the extent of capacity utilization in the Canadian economy, that is to say, the extent to which there are factories which are not being used fully to produce goods and the extent to which there are facilities which are not being used fully to produce and distribute services in the Canadian economy. The facts are clear. There is a very high rate of unused industrial capacity in the country, and this Bill does nothing whatsoever to bring about the increased usage of the unused industrial capacity.
Another factor is the rate of profit which is already being earned, or expected to be earned, by business in Canada. There are many in the business community who feel that there has not been a sufficient recovery in profits from the lows which they reached during the recession to justify vastly increased new investments. There is nothing in the Bill to increase the rate of return, or the prospects of an improved rate of return, for business in Canada which would lead business to decide to make further investments in the Canadian economy.
In addition, one of the problems which business has been given for not being willing to increase investment in Canada is the high rate of debt that has been built up and which clutters the balance sheets of business in the country. It is a hangover

January 29, 1985
Investment Canada Act
from the last recession. Until business feels that there is a better ratio in its balance sheets between debt and assets, and until the debt situation is under better control, business will continue to be inhibited when it comes to investment decisions. I reiterate that the Investment Canada Bill does nothing to help the problem of excessive debt which still clutters the balance sheets of too many companies in Canada.
We do not simply want to see more investment from abroad; we want to see more investment by Canadians so that they will have the opportunity to benefit from the development of the resources, capacities and skills which are found in their country. Canadians have the wherewithal to invest more fully in Canada, if one looks at the very high level of savings as a percentage of the Gross National Product. Canada has a rate of savings which is somewhat greater than, and possibly double, that of the rate of savings in the United States. There is nothing in the Bill which would bring about increased opportunities for investment in the economy by Canadians. There is nothing in the Bill to encourage Canadians to use their high level of savings to invest in Canadian opportunities. Although the Bill gives some superficial lip service to the idea of encouraging investment, there is nothing in it to bring about that concrete result when it comes to investment by Canadians or investment by other people.
There has been no indication to the Opposition or to Canadians generally in the speeches of government Members in the debate on second reading thus far that this Bill will bring about the flow of investment which the Government says will result, the kind of investment which continues to be needed to create jobs and bring about an expansion of the Canadian economy. Spokesmen for business who were quoted in the press, including a recent article in the Financial Post, continue to confirm that the level of investment expected in this country will be weak compared to the level at which it was in past years under Liberal Governments.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the amendment before this House should be rejected so that government Members will have a better opportunity to make their case as to what this Bill will accomplish for Canada, because they have not made that case as yet. In fact, they have not done anything to undermine the basic point which I and others have made, that is that this Investment Canada Bill, rather than bringing benefits to Canadians in terms of jobs, investment, research and development, will have just the opposite effect. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, until the Government can persuade us and the Canadian people in this second reading debate that this Bill deserves to go forward, it should not do so. The second reading debate should continue and this motion should be soundly rejected.

Mr. Speaker, what we are dealing with here is a Bill which has been fairly called "a Bill to sell our country out". It is no wonder that the Government is in such a hurry to end the debate with a gag motion. It would rather that Canadians do not hear that this Bill will in effect
help foreign businessmen, especially from the major trading partner, the United States, to come in, buy up our businesses and then shut them down as was done at the Black and Decker plant.
We do not need this Bill. We do not need to weaken FIRA; we need to strengthen it and make it more like the anti-dumping tribunal. We need an opportunity for public representations to be made on the question of a takeover by the company which wants to do so, stating its position and reasons and what it will commit itself to do for the country from which it proposes to make a profit. We need statements from the workers and statements from the communities which will be affected. There would then be an opportunity for new commitments to be worked out or, at the least, an opportunity for the community to know what its future is.
However, this Bill does not propose anything of the sort. Instead, this Bill follows the line taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in the fall and the Minister who moved it, "that Canada needs foreign cash", and there is the unspoken statement that, "we will do anything at all to get it on a short-term basis". The device which is being used now is to make the review more secret, more limited-in fact, limited to one man. That is not what we need, Mr. Speaker. That is how we got into our present trouble.
There has been a great rush of foreign investment into Canada ever since 1945, the end of World War II. I remember that when we came out of the Forces the slogan was "full employment". We all remembered the dirty thirties, we all remembered the hobos riding on the railway cars going east and going west, all of them looking for jobs which were not there. I remember our church collecting pots and pans for a desperate family who were going back to some piece of farm land in Manitoba that was so poor it was empty at the time. I remember my half brother, Bill, working in the Winnipeg soup kitchen. He thought he was lucky to have the opportunity to work the midnight shift as a cleaner, and talked about the men slashing their wrists. I remember my Dad saying to a neighbour, "If war was declared today, I guess you'd have a job tomorrow". In 1945 we did not want to go back to that. So the doors were opened wide to foreign investment which was supposed to be the solution to our problems. During that period, when foreign investment ruled, unemployment rose from less than 3 per cent to about 12 per cent. Unemployment quadrupled in this land during the four decades when foreign investment ruled. It was a short-range solution, or what some people have called a quick fix. It apparently worked for a few years, and now we are having the long-term pain for that short-term gain. Canada was mortgaged to the United States.
This massive increase of foreign investment meant that there was no commitment to keeping Canadian plants open. We had forgotten what happened in the 1930s when foreign owners shut down their plants in Canada, because for a few years Canada and the U.S. were almost the only countries in the world able to sell manufactured products after World War

II. Things looked easy. We did not understand what was coming until the late 1950s. Under the Diefenbaker Government, the last Tory Government which lasted for more than a few months, we had tight money, bankruptcies, and rising unemployment. Remember how immigrants were harassed in the name of unemployment? All the while the U.S. was taking over our industries, so that now they own or control 51 per cent of our manufacturing and we have lost hundreds of thousands of jobs in the last couple of years. They own 98 per cent of the rubber industry and 51 per cent of agriculture. When I grew up in Canada I understood that this was an agricultural country. One thing Canadians could do was to feed ourselves and others. Now we have lost control of 51 per cent of Canadian agriculture and there is nothing to say that we will not be in the position of some other countries some day when the food is grown here but exported while Canadians go hungry.
Some 92 per cent of transportation equipment, 70 per cent of electrical products and 71 per cent of chemicals are controlled by the U.S.
Therefore, the top 50 companies in Canada can be analysed this way. U.S.-owned companies lost twice as many jobs in Canada as Canadian-owned companies during 1982 and 1983. Why? Of firms with over 500 employees it has been found that the Canadian-owned firms spent ten times as big a proportion of their profits on research and development as the foreign-owned companies did. Graduates of the University of Toronto are hunting for jobs, and the reason for the cut-back in research jobs is that the foreign owned companies do not do their research in Canada. Yet the Minister proposes to open the way for more takeovers and he does not want the U of T graduates to know what he is doing in time to protest.
Foreign firms are pumping money out of Canada. The U.S. companies, which represent 36 per cent of all corporate assets here, account for 61 per cent of remittances abroad. In other words, when small business is looking for capital we are being starved by the foreign-owned industries. One third of the tax revenue which should have come to us from the computer manufacturing industry was diverted by companies which played the international pricing game between factories.
We are not, Mr. Speaker, getting what was promised to us in this American takeover of Canadian industries. They are not creating more jobs. For a few years after World War II it appeared to be so, but in fact it is not so, and that is why we have been in such severe trouble for the last three or four years. We do not need an increased takeover of our factories which, as the previous speaker pointed out, are not even operating at full capacity. A foreigner owner would be happy to shut them down completely, probably. What we need is greater protection of the Canadian worker and potential owner of industry who wants to develop industries which will work here in Canada and create jobs for Canadians.
The experience of other countries is just like that of Canada but more intensive. It has gone further because they were weaker to start with. Take a country like the Philippines. In 10 years of this kind of program, foreign control of investment
Investment Canada Act
capital and the import-export policies of their government, they have had their real wages cut in half. Workers with only half the money cannot pay the price for rice, which means that the price of rice going to the farmers was cut in half. The result in the Philippines was poverty, repression, assassination, and riots. We are not close to that in Canada yet. We have only growing poverty and some hints of repression through the secret service Bill of the last Government.
This has not been happening only in the Philippines. The same process was carried on in the same years in South Korea and in Central and South America under the rule of the International Monetary Fund. In all cases there were Governments in place which agreed to allow growing foreign takeovers of industries, either directly or through loans from the IMF and western banks. In all cases unemployment and poverty have grown to desperate proportions. In all cases they are looking at possible bankruptcies.
We do not need this gag motion to end this debate. We need to let the public know what is happening.

Mr. Speaker, Tuesday, December 11, 1984 will live as a day of infamy. On that day the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) introduced Bill C-15, an Act respecting investment in Canada to be read a second time and referred to committee. With those and many other words he set out to dismantle the progress that we have made over the decades to make this country a place where greater control is held by Canadian entrepreneurs and workers.
January 28, 1985, yesterday, will also be remembered as a day of betrayal. On that day the Government and the Tory Party undertook to invoke closure to prevent this debate from continuing so that we would not be able to discuss what was at stake with this most important issue. Some feel that this may challenge the very independence of Canada. Those of us in the Opposition know that it will threaten our independence as a nation and affect our sovereignty. Therefore, a great deal is at stake in this debate.
When the Tory Party was in opposition it was very jealous of its right to debate every Bill at great length. The members spoke of the importance of freedom of information, consultation and dialogue. We now see that that same Tory Party, which was on this side of the Flouse such a short time ago, has already betrayed the promises it made to the electorate of Canada that it would form an open government ready to listen and debate. Unlike the Liberal Government, it was going to take its time and listen to people's opinions. Already, such a short time after the opening of the House of Commons, although we have passed quite a number of Bills, we see on this vital Bill impatience to choke off debate in the House of Commons. It is rather sad to see them try to silence the voice of a small Opposition which is trying to sound a note of caution and concern on behalf of a large number of Canadians who have supported this program for years with their votes

January 29, 1985
Investment Canada Act
and views. This is no unimportant matter and therefore does deserve the serious consideration of the House of Commons.
We now discover that we will be unable to carry on this debate. Unfortunately, in the Conservative's presentation on this important subject, they have been misrepresenting the facts about FIRA and the effects of the Foreign Investment Review Act on Canada. We believe that we have ample evidence to show that it has had a beneficial effect on Canada and a beneficial effect on Canadians.
Let us look at the facts as shown by the statistics. In the ten years prior to the inception of FIRA, from 1964 to 1973, new direct foreign investment in the form of takeovers and other transactions flowed into Canada at a rate of approximately $700 million per annum. Since FIRA has been in force, from 1974 to 1984, the average has been about $1.4 billion per year rather than $700 million. This represents a substantial increase in investments since the time FIRA came into effect.
Over the past four years, the new direct foreign investment figures averaged over $2 billion. In 1983 alone, interest rates were seen as being historically high in comparison to U.S. rates especially. As well, larger firms were retrenching and rationalizing and pulling back. There was a long-term net capital inflow into Canada of $2.8 billion in that difficult year. The facts just simply do not bear out this mythology that has been set forth by the Tory Party about the dangers of FIRA.
As a matter of fact, although the Conservatives often refer to $17 billion in equity capital that has left the country since the introduction of the National Energy Program, the truth of the matter is that over this period there was an aggregate net capital inflow to Canada of $21 billion.
Although it is true that there was an outflow of money from Canada as a result of the NEP, it is largely the result of successful takeover bids by Canadian firms for foreign-owned oil subsidiaries, which considerably increased Canadian ownership of the oil and gas industry. Those who are doubtful need only consider the fact that the Canadian ownership of the petroleum industry has increased considerably during that period for a relatively small outflow of funds.
It cost us money to buy back what we believe we deserve to own, and Canadians supported that buy-back as well as the idea that Canadians should exploit their own country and derive a major benefit from the resources that belong to Canada. We do not apologize at all for that reality.
Moreover, since 1974, the Foreign Investment Review Agency has approved 92 per cent of all applications. Procedures were streamlined in the June, 1982, budget and the approval rate is currently around 97 per cent. That can hardly be called a stringent discouragement to foreign investment.
FIRA exists to ensure that foreign investment will benefit Canada and Canadians and it achieves this by considering the potential investments in a number of dimensions, such as the effects of foreign investment on economic activity, the degree
of participation by Canadians, and provincial needs and compatibility with national industrial policies.
All through FIRA's existence, the federal Government has consulted with the provinces on every foreign investment application. Rather than some arbitrary action, it has consulted with the provinces on every application. In the past nine years, the provinces have disagreed with the federal Government on less than 3 per cent of investment applications.
Although most countries do not have a centralized foreign investment review system, they certainly do not have an open door policy on foreign investment. Many countries, including the United States, review investment with legislative provisions and administrative procedures. Canada is one of the few countries in the world that openly outlines investment regulations.
A recent study by the Brooking Institution shows that 35 per cent of U.S. manufactured goods are protected by quotas and buy-American rules and other non-tariff restrictions. It also shows that this protection in the United States has risen by 15 per cent in the last three years of the Reagan rule. While our boy scouts in the Tory Government do their good deeds for the United States and open the door to the U.S. and foreign investors, the Government has had the door slammed in its face by U.S. protectionism.
We regard this kind of debate as vital to our independence, our sovereignty and the interests of our people. We are concerned about unemployment and the fact that foreign takeovers close plants in this country and throw people out of work overnight. We regard this debate as one that should continue and one in which the Government should explain why our anxieties are unfounded and prove to us what it will do to protect Canadians from these dangers. I am deeply disappointed that the Government sees Fit to cut off this debate on one of the most important topics that the House of Commons could consider.

Mr. Speaker, it is rather disillusioning to be taking part in a debate on an issue which Canadians believe their national Government began to address more than a decade ago with the establishment of the Foreign Investment Review Agency. At that time Canadians believed the federal Government was addressing the issue of domination of the Canadian economy, primarily by the United States.
If members of the Conservative Party believe that Canadians are no longer concerned about foreign domination of our economy as well as of other areas, they are entirely wrong. I cannot understand how the Conservatives could have gone through an election campaign without realizing that one of the most important assurances that young Canadians wanted was that Canada will remain an independent nation with its own salience on the international scene. Perhaps they view this Bill as salutory if they think there might be great economic opportunities for them in becoming totally integrated with the U.S. economy and becoming almost entirely a branch plant economy. However, they should also take into account the
January 29, 1985

realization that a Bill such as this will not in fact provide them with the economic opportunities they seek. All our young people feel, and they are right in feeling, that they are in a horrific double-bind. There is no longer any pride in Canada and no longer any hope for jobs and economic opportunities.
When the Foreign Investment Review Agency was set up, there was a feeling that at last Canada would have, at least in theory, a mechanism to ensure that some benefit to Canadians was derived from the domination of our resource industries and our secondary and manufacturing industries by multinationals. It is unfortunate that FIRA was never very clear on how to hold foreign countries to commitments to Canadian economic development. In fact, foreign ownership that FIRA allowed did not, as we know from reading all the statistics, provide very much, if any, real new investment in Canada. It was the case time and time again of foreign multinationals buying out existing Canadian companies and not creating new investment. Often they bought them out with our money, money they borrowed from Canadian banks, and did not create any new investment or any new jobs.
We argued many times over the past several years that there must be a genuine commitment from a foreign company to create real new investment and new jobs before the company is allowed to enter Canada, and that the commitment should be closely monitored. At least with all its failings we did have, and Canadians were proud that we had, a review agency that did not simply say that Canada is totally up for sale to foreign interests. It is disheartening for us in the New Democratic Party to witness the dismantling of the Foreign Investment Review Agency, and it is even more disheartening for us to hear the Government, when it tries to justify this measure, which these days is not very often, do so on the grounds that the foreign investment this Bill hopes to attract will somehow, without any controls over its use, provide jobs for Canadians.
As I have said, we know from our own past experience that without any controls or commitments no new jobs are provided for Canadians. If you look at the comments of my colleagues in this party, Mr. Speaker, you will see that they have repeatedly pointed out that of the top 50 companies in Canada the greatest number of jobs lost over the past two years has been from U.S.-owned companies.
One would think that if the Conservatives wanted to put a new face on old economic policies and if they wanted not to be seen entirely as the captives of international capitalism, they would propose something like the joint venture schemes in which we see countries like Sweden, Italy, China, and many others engaged. In those countries very serious and very important controls are exercised over foreign capital. Foreign capital is joined by domestic capital, and the domestic firm usually retains ownership or a significant ownership of the company engaged in the joint venture. As far as I know, the Government has not examined the joint venture operations that now exist in countries like Sweden, Italy, China, and even the United States.
Investment Canada Act
I was looking at developments in the last year in the U.S. auto industry. I found that a large number of U.S. firms have joined forces with Japanese firms to manufacture products and components in Japan. The reverse is also occurring. Honda is making cars in Ohio and Nissan is making trucks in Tennessee. Hundreds of Japanese high-tech companies are entering into supply contracts with U.S. companies, opening plants, building laboratories, and funding research in the United States. This trend is forcing even the U.S. Government to prod companies doing business in the U.S. to invest in complex production using American workers, ensuring minimum employment levels and retaining research and development facilities. Why don't the Conservatives at least look at that kind of operation, at that kind of control of the operations of multinationals in Canada rather than simply giving away the whole shop? The Conservatives could get commitment for real new investment and real new jobs, but there is nothing in this Bill that makes it possible for such commitments to be extracted from multinational companies. The government obviously continues to be a puppet of international capitalism, just as it is of Cold War diplomacy.

This is coming from a political Party that over the years in opposition decried not only the use of closure, but also the allocation of time. In this case we do not even have an allocation of time.

-but in fact the effect of this motion is to close debate. I know that there is another closure procedure under another Standing Order, but this one has the same effect. It does in effect close off a very important debate.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) when he went to New York after the tabling of this Bill announced that Canada was now open for business. Again, that is a lot of rhetoric. Anyone who looks at the statistics and the record over the last year or two will see that the volume of business between Canada and the United States has been enormous. As a matter of fact, the balance of trade in favour of Canada has been so high that the United States Government is very concerned. We have been selling very strongly into the U.S. market and making a lot of profits, and the Americans have been selling into our market as well. It is not a question of being open for business with the United States. It is, as many people have said and as our Leader has said, a question now of whether we are going to sell out the country to the United States and other foreign interests.
Many government people have tried to give the impression that FIRA, the Foreign Investment Review Agency, was against foreign investment, but that is not the case. The purpose of FIRA was to ensure by review that all investment in Canada was in the best interests of Canada and of the Canadian people.
Why was such legislation necessary a number of years ago? It was necessary because the pattern at that time had been that when foreign companies took over Canadian firms or invested in a substantial way in Canada, they were doing several things that were against our interests. In many cases they were closing down the research and development being carried out by Canadian firms. All that research and development went to their head offfices, whether they were in Chicago, New York or London, England.
I remind members of the Conservative Party from Montreal of the example of Ayerst McKenna, a long-time prominent pharmaceutical firm which was bought by a U.S. company. It went about gradually closing down the research and development area of Ayerst McKenna in Montreal, leaving many highly skilled scientists and researchers out of work. If it had not been for the actions of the federal Government and the Quebec Government last year in setting up research facilities under the reconstruction program, many of those scientists would have been obliged to go to the United States to find work. That is one reason.
Another reason was that many American-owned or other foreign-owned firms shut down the manufacturing element altogether in Canada and did the entire manufacturing in their plants in the foreign countries. They simply kept a sales agency in Canada to sell the U.S.-produced products.
There were many other negative effects. There was the siphoning off of profits into the United States and other foreign countries. The obligation was put on the Canadian subsidiary Firms to follow U.S. national interests in politics.
We had examples of that during the OPEC crisis and also with respect to our relations with Cuba.
In tabling this Bill, government Members have said that this Investment Canada Bill and the dismantling of FIRA will produce jobs. It will have the opposite effect. If there is no way of screening the foreign investment, no way to negotiate with the foreign investors in Canada and no way to oblige them to ensure that the investment is in the best interests of Canada, they will close down the research and development and the manufacturing and simply use the shell in Canada to sell their products. Therefore, there will be fewer jobs instead of more.
A good thing about FIRA was the way it operated to negotiate a better deal for Canada. As many debaters have pointed out, 92 per cent of the applications were approved. It was not that a large number of applications for investment were turned down. It does not show up in these statistics, but many of us know because we were part of the process over the years. Because FIRA was there, the investing company knew that its proposal had to contain elements which would be in the best interests of Canada. It was always conscious of the fact that it could not buy out a Canadian firm or invest in Canada without considering what was in the best interests of this country. There was a deterrent effect in the law which obliged it to consider those factors at all times.
If a foreign company did not do that, rather than turn down the investment proposal altogether, very often the Government would negotiate with the investment applicant and say, "We do not think your application does enough for Canada. We want some assurance that you will buy your supplies from Canadian suppliers. We want some assurance that you will keep research and development in Canada. We want some asssurance that you will maintain the manufacturing element". Very often through the negotiations they would make a commitment to do that, and the application would be approved. In the statistics on applications approved and rejected that was not always shown, but it was a very important element in the operations of FIRA which provided benefits for Canada and for Canadian jobs.
Bill C-15 is only one part of a Conservative government program to weaken considerably Canada's economic, political and cultural independence. When you look at the cut-backs with respect to the CBC and the cultural agencies and when you see how this Government has been kowtowing to the United States with respect to the defence and external affairs policy, simply going along with the star wars research and so on, you see that in the long run, this country is in for some great difficulty. We will not have the institutions or the laws to maintain those things that we as Canadians think are important.
Over a hundred years ago we decided to be a country on our own. We did not want to be American or British. We recently adopted a new Constitution. We want to be Canadians, despite the fact we are only 25 million spread along thousands of miles of border, next to a huge giant with over 200 million people. If we did not have special laws and institutions like the CBC, national railways, national airlines and FIRA, we would be
January 29, 1985

completely taken over and submerged by the massive U.S. economy, political system, culture and so on. That is not what Canadians expect or want.
We do not have the numbers on this side to defeat or amend this Bill, but through debates such as this we hope to influence public opinion outside this House so that that public will approach the 211 Conservative Members of Parliament and tell them how they feel about Canadian sovereignty, economics, culture and politics and that they will put pressure on them. We also hope to stimulate Canadian groups, individuals, professors and writers to appear before the parliamentary committee once this Bill gets there and let us know what they think about this measure.
My time is up. This is a very short debate because of the closure motion. I urge the Government to reconsider many of the elements of this Bill and give heed to common sense in what is a very important matter.

Mr. Speaker, I rise a second time on Bill C-15, the first time on the closure matter. I wish to mention some of the fundamental principles, not only of the New Democratic Party but also of business that I feel are being ignored and even violated in Bill C-15.
There is no inherent hostility or hostility per se on the part of the NDP toward the United States or U.S. capital. There is no inherent fundamental quarrel with some of the practices that American companies bring to this country, practices which have been successful in their country and within their business environment. There is no quarrel with U.S. methods of marketing, although I am sure that Members on both sides of the House have felt that techniques that were being imported, particularly as they relate to politics, were somewhat overstated and excessive, given the Canadian environment and our traditions of moderation and caution. Nevertheless, our neighbours to the south have, in general, produced things that work. When they find something that works, they stick with it.
I would emphasize and re-emphasize that we are not seeking in this debate today to present some sort of front or attitude of antipathy toward U.S. capital, corporations or management practices. We are seeking to affirm and re-affirm Canadian economic traditions. It is our belief that in proposing Bill C-15, the Government has been seduced by U.S. propaganda at both the political and the business levels. That propaganda is aimed-and here again we allege no great conspiracy, but merely a community of interests that did not need the specific mechanisms stated-at enabling our neighbours to the south to buy Canadian resources, companies and assets at a price more in their interest than in the interest of Canada. That, Mr. Speaker, is of course a familiar business technique. It is not one that is inherently, essentially or fundamentally immoral, but it is nevertheless a business technique and it is one which is being aided and abetted by the present Government.
We did not find that the Foreign Investment Review Agency was an unusual mechanism. If we look at the legislative
Investment Canada Act
structures and commercial regulations of such countries as Japan, for example, we find that there are mechanisms in place which provide for a much more extensive and thorough review and analysis of attempted foreign investments than did the Foreign Investment Review Agency.
One of my colleagues made a good point yesterday, and it is one that should have been taken to heart by the Government. He stated that the United States itself very definitely does have a foreign investment review agency which goes by the style and title of the American Congress. The American Congress is accustomed-and who would deny it the right to do so-to reviewing foreign presence in its economy, but not only foreign presence in the sense of foreign investment or foreign purchases of U.S. companies but also, and perhaps more insidiously, foreign presence in the matter of imports. Let there be no mistake. The commercial regime under which the United States operates is far more invidious in both a qualitative and quantitative fashion to the Canadian economy and Canadian business than the Foreign Investment Review Agency, the National Energy Program and the national policy ever were to U.S. interests operating in Canada.
In tabling this legislation, the Government is sending a message to the marketplace and it is a very unfortunate message. It is a message that is being sent in conjunction with the planned sale of Crown corporations. It was only partly with tongue in cheek that I characterized that planned sale in my maiden speech last week as an attempt to set up a fire sale of Canada. We saw the spectacle of the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) snapping eagerly at an initial tentative approach made by the B.C. Resources Investment Corporation to take over a couple of Crown corporations that were on the block. I characterized that apparent interest by the B.C. Resources Investment Corporation as a logical step off a tall building. The proposed purchaser did not have the assets, the commercial background or the track record to take on the Crown corporations in which the Hon. Minister supposed it might be interested.
The Government has not given any assurance to the House that the Crown corporations that are put up for sale will be available only to Canadian investors or Canadian corporations. The absence of that assurance along with the legislation that has been put before us will, to my way of thinking, create an expectation in the United States that Americans can indeed bid on Canadian Crown corporations that are coming on the block and that they will be able to pick up those Crown corporations at a price which will serve their interests better than the interests of the Canadian taxpayers.
In tabling the Investment Canada Bill, the Government is discarding an honourable and historical tradition of Canadian economic nationalism in which the Progressive Conservative Party and its predecessors have indeed participated. Why is there today a railway that does run from sea to shining sea? Why was the last spike driven at Craigellachie in 1886? The railway exists and that last spike was driven in order to tie together a country. It happened because the predecessors of the present Government at least had the wisdom to believe and

Investment Canada Act
know that a government that did not control the economic links which held its country together was a government which would not be able to plan adequately for the economy and would not be able adequately to influence, guide, mould and direct the future economic development of its country.
I believe that the facts speak for themselves. We saw that the national policy was indeed a successful one. It is my belief that while the links of our economic fabric today may not be so obvious, tangible and concrete as was the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway in 1886, those links nevertheless are of equal importance today as they were 100 years ago.
This tradition of economic nationalism was not established with blinkers on. It was not established for mere reasons of political expediency. It was not established for the sake of simply being different and using different mechanisms. It was established for very good reasons, reasons of Canadian nationhood and, yes, reasons of Canadian patriotism to which regionalism can contribute as well as operate against. It was established for legitimate reasons and deserves continuation for those same reasons.
The Provinces of Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba and British Columbia all recognized that only through provincial control of its utilities could the provinces have a real say in the direction, support and development of provincial growth. That is why we have-

speechtext: I regret to interrupt the Hon. Member but his time has expired. Is the House ready for the question?

Mr. Speaker, when I spoke on this Bill previously, I brought forward some concerns that had come from Atlantic Canada, specifically concerns in relation to the fishing industry. Since that time, those concerns have become even greater among those employed in the fishing industry. There are concerns over what effect this Bill may have on foreign takeovers, because most fish plant operations are tied to quota licences. In effect, those quotas could be taken over by foreign companies and they could be used in whatever fashion a foreign company decided. For instance, it could close down a plant if it was seen as being in competition with that in its own mother country, it could reduce the operations or indeed, I suppose, in some cases it could even expand the operations, and that would be good. However, that is not likely to be the case.
I have also expressed my concern regarding the management of Investment Canada. I have expressed my concern over the fact that one Minister is responsible for deciding what is good for Canada and what is not good for Canada. I have some very grave concerns about that process. Under FIR A, there was a representative Cabinet committee which made the final decisions. I think it is imperative that all regions of the country including Atlantic Canada, the Northwest Territories and western Canada, should have input into the decisions that are made, and particulary as to how any investment may affect those regions.
In the last few days, we have seen just how Government works. There is no recourse to the bilateral West Coast salmon agreement with the U.S. which the Minister was able to initial. It is very difficult to discuss that openly with the different parts of the industry which are involved. They have no input into that decision. I realize it is sometimes difficult in that governments are required to make decisions, but where is the appropriate consultation which would provide those sectors of the fishing industry-be it the sports Fishery, the trawler associations or whatever-and the people who are directly affected with an opportunity to have an input into this agreement? There is a danger in having a one-man operation in government. I do not think we can sufficiently stress that danger.
If we look at the track record of foreign investors in Canada, we will find that it has not always been good. I believe that Canada has lost in research and development. Most research and development of foreign companies which operate in Canada is done outside of Canada. Research and development creates very important jobs in the Canadian economy. Those jobs benefit our university graduates. We cannot always ship our brains outside of Canada. There must be a way in which meaningful jobs can be created, not just the ordinary jobs which last six to eight weeks. We must encourage jobs of a high-paying nature.
Dangers in the high technology industries are posed with the Investment Canada Bill. I am not the only one who believes that. In the business section of The Toronto Star today, Mr. James Gillies, a professor of policy and director of the Max Bell program in business and government studies in the Faculty of Administrative Studies at York University, who was a long-time Progressive Conservative member of this House, said:
Also contributing to the balance of payments problem has been the inflow of foreign capital. It is imperative that capital flowing into the country be used for productive purposes and not for the transfer of the ownership of assets which does nothing for the economy and simply contributes to the foreign exchange problem.
Mr. Gillies has pointed out very clearly that foreign capital has not always been beneficial to the country. He went on to
say:
Not all foreign investment is productive. It is naive to believe that any flow of capital into the country will move the economy forward. It depends entirely on what it is used for. If it is not invested in the production of new plant and equipment and does not lead to an increase in exports it can have serious negative economic consequences.
Moreover, until the intractable balance of payments problem is solved we must try to limit the borrowing of capital from abroad. No government or government agency should borrow in foreign markets under current conditions. If a government has a function that it believes must be performed either directly or through a government agency, the capital should be raised domestically or the proposed operation should be postponed.
Mr. Gillies-and I am sure we all have a great respect for his views-is saying that this is not necessarily a good thing. However, the Party to which he used to belong is bulldozing this piece of legislation through the House.

It is one thing to create a job-and we want to create jobs in Canada-but we should not do that by sacrificing the jobs which are already in the economy. What is the benefit if foreign investment enters Canada and takes over a company which will put other companies out of business? That is what worries me about the structure of this Bill.
Again, with respect to the one-man operation of the Bill, how will it provide proper input for other businesses in order that this can have an idea of what is going on? It is similar to a closed shop. There should be an amendment which requires the decisions to be made public. Canadian investors virtually could be wiped out overnight by the decision of one person, a decision which is in direct competition with their operations.
I mentioned previously some of the problems in the fishery in the Atlantic provinces. The National Farmers Union is very concerned about Investment Canada because of the development of mock products and certainly the new products which are made from whey milk. It is very detrimental to the dairy industry of Canada. The same thing is happening in the fishery with the introduction of mock crabmeat.
I see that my time is running out. Ten minutes is not long enough to put forward our views on the Bill and the seriousness with which this Bill should be taken by the Government and by Members of Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to explore the whole question of how we approach investment capital in Canada as it relates to foreign investment. If there is a company which requires human capital and that company wishes to go outside of Canada's borders to get that human capital-in other words a worker-this Government, as did the last, requires the company to do a job search. In other words, the company must search for that human capital from sea to sea to ensure that there is no out-of-work Canadian who could perform the task for which there is a vacancy. We should take the same approach when it comes to out-of-work capital. If we are in need of an infusion of capital into a business concern in Canada, whether it is partial or total, a capital search throughout Canada should be required. I believe the Government's role is to facilitate that.
I raised that idea with the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Bissonnette) in the finance committee meeting last night, in the context of whether or not that was the role of the Federal Business Development Bank. While he indicated that it was not its role to work with FIRA to search for capital, when FIRA receives a request from a Canadian firm to allow it to sell to a U.S. company or other foreign company, he thought it was a good idea that perhaps we should consider.
In order to highlight that, I would like to refer to the recent announcement of approvals which were made by the Foreign Investment Review Agency which appeared in The Globe and Mail issue of today. It was indicated there that 38 proposals were approved. The article gives some indication of the kind of things which we are allowing foreign money to be used for. We are allowing a company from Rockford, Illinois, to acquire control of a Canadian business which imports, distributes and
Investment Canada Act
services air compressors. Surely Canadians can do that. We do not have to have someone from Illinois come and do it for us. We do not need anyone from Hartford, Connecticut to acquire control of a Canadian business which imports and sells thread and mill rolling dies and machines. We can do that. We have the skills and the knowledge. Obviously, a Canadian company was already doing it and, for whatever reason, it found itself in need of capital whether because the owner was retiring and wanted to get out of the business or because its capital needs were beyond its capabilities. We should be going to that company and saying, "What can we do to help you? What can we do to ensure that your company can remain Canadian-owned?"
A company in Dallas, Texas, was given permission to acquire control of a business in western Canada which sells prescription eye glasses, contact lenses and related eye care products. A company from Portland, Oregon, was given permission to acquire a Canadian company which manufactures band saws for the wood products industry. The last thing we should do, Mr. Speaker, is to let another foreign interest get involved in our manufacturing sector. We have the skills and the capacity to produce our own machinery for the harvesting of our own wood and for the mining of our own ore. We do not have to go outside our borders to find capital. We should work within our borders.
We in this Party have freely admitted that from time to time there are needs for foreign capital to come in to start up new enterprises, because sometimes there are just no Canadians who are prepared to take the risk, for whatever reason. However, one case just boggles my mind. Can you believe, Mr. Speaker, that permission has been given to a company from San Antonio, Texas, to come into Canada and operate a cattle ranch? That is beyond reason. Surely there are Canadians who have the wherewithal to do this. We have been operating cattle ranches in western Canada for years. We do not need Texans coming in to do it for us. Perhaps that is an indication of the lack of support given to the farming and cattle raising communities.
The rationale, Mr. Speaker, is that we should not be opening our doors through Investment Canada and allowing foreign dollars to come in at will. We should be looking at our rules with regard to foreign investment and asking ourselves how we can ensure that Canadians are safeguarded, that there is no unnecessary acquisition, and that there will be no investment in areas where Canadians have the wherewithal and the financial ability to do it themselves. On the other hand, we should make sure that when there are investments, they do bring about real benefits, not just to the investor but to the workers and to the community. We must make sure there is some protection. I admit that FIRA was not the best of vehicles. It certainly was not put together the way we would have liked.
In my own riding and in the riding of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp), FIRA approved the acquisition by Canada Safeway (Ltd.,) I think it

Investment Canada Act
was, of Dominion Stores Limited, and one of the conditions was that the store in Thunder Bay must be closed. It is wrong for the Government to tell a business to rationalize, and the better way is not to do so through Investment Canada. We should not just throw the doors wide open. We have to ensure that there is control over our own destiny and that whatever dollars are spent are used for the benefit of Canadians.
The Federal Business Development Bank has an excellent program of equity investment which allows it to take shares in companies which are in need of some extra financing but are unable to deal with the burden of a loan situation. The Government is then allowed to sell the shares back to them. In fact, it is required over a period of time to sell the shares back to the company. So in that way the company is given some bridging, some time to get on its feet and become a profitable operation once again. I think that is what we should be doing, Mr. Speaker. We should be using tools like the FBDB to help Canadian entrepreneurs survive and develop so that we can grow as a country and make sure that our prosperity is our children's prosperity.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Grand Bay-White Falls-Labrador.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, you came very close and I congratulate you. It is Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador. I know that was an inadvertent slip on your part.
I am pleased with having the opportunity to rise and speak on this Bill once more, Mr. Speaker, because I believe it is important to put on the record some of the same points and possibly a few more than I did last time. I feel that the people in my province should know that the legislation we are being asked to deal with now is not of paramount importance. It has no urgency, and we should be dealing with other far more meaningful legislation. The fact is that there is really no need for this Bill at this time. It is fluff, cotton candy, smoke and mirrors, public relations. FIRA, indeed, was working. If one checks The Globe and Mail one will find that over 90 per cent of the applications which came before Cabinet and before FIRA were approved. So we do not need this legislation in order to keep out or bring in United States capital. It is really not going to make any difference one way or the other.
But suppose this Bill did attract foreign capital to Canada? What is more important, it seems to me, is for the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) to tell us how he is going to target that capital, whether from outside or inside of Canada, to the various regions of the country. I feel that that is the greater challenge. How can we ensure that the East, the West and the North get this capital? That is what the Minister has not told us. Are there going to be tax incentives? The Minister has changed the DRIE program already. He said, for example, that the tourist industry will no longer be eligible for grants and loans under DRIE, the regional industrial development program. What incentives of any kind is the Minister going to bring before us to make sure that investment, whether foreign or Canadian, goes to the various underdeveloped regions of the country? That is not what is before us and that is what should be before us now.
The Minister should tell us how regional development is going to be carried out. What is his policy with regard to regional development? We only know so far from this Government that what it does want is for the private sector to replace the public sector. We have no quarrel with that. It is a laudable objective. But how do you ensure that it happens? The only thing my area of the country has received from this Government so far as proof of its good will and as proof of the effectiveness of its policy, is cut-backs in funds which we have depended on for years, for decades and possibly even for generations. I say that not out of pride but because it is realistic.
The whole thrust so far of government policy in the east has been to take away things we have. Let us look at what has been cut back. For example, there has been a reduction in expenditures in the fisheries infrastructure. There were wharves, breakwaters, haul-outs and facilities on land for fishermen in Newfoundland, in Labrador and in the Atlantic Provinces, which were supposed to go ahead but which did not? Spending has been reduced on the fisheries infrastructure.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made a commitment to the forestry industry in Corner Brook during the election campaign. Yet that public sector spending has not gone ahead. Mr. Crosbie is suggesting that a minimum-medium security prison which was committed to central Newfoundland, in my own riding, may not go ahead. He says he cannot find the money for it although the money was there. Mr. Crosbie is now saying that possibly the Government will renege on that commitment.

There is no justice in cutting out something we have had for years before putting something in its place. We do not put the cart before the horse. If the Minister of Justice were truly interested in justice, he would see that justice is done in my riding and in my province. That is the whole point.
We have not seen that justice has been done up until now. There have been cut-backs in the CBC, particularly in the northern areas. I said before and I say again that if the Government really wants to do something about our cultural heritage, it will see that those cut-backs are cancelled. Grants for pure research and applied research have been cut back. We are going to lose expert scientists from the only university we have in Newfoundland because of these cut-backs. There is no way that applied research can flourish unless pure research

flourishes. The two go hand in hand, and these cut-backs are going to have an immediate effect on job creation. Even more, they will have a serious effect on long-term job creation because the new technology will not be there. There have been cut-backs in unemployment insurance at a time when unemployment is at its highest. That is the record so far and the only thing I have to go by.
In the meantime, Mr. Speaker, we know that ferry rates in the Atlantic area have been raised. Of course this has the effect of driving up all prices. Whether it is the producer or the consumer, there is an additional financial burden on people in the Atlantic area.
What is going to replace the public sector spending which has been cut? Is there going to be new private sector capital coming from Japan, the United States or Great Britain? We do not really care where it comes from. Is it going to the forest industry? The record so far of British capital in my area is a sorry one. British capital is letting plants go to ruin, not allowing them to keep up and be competitive. That is the record of British capital in Newfoundland. Are we going to see new capital in the fishery? We have not seen it so far. Indeed, the Government has had to step in and provide the needed capital. Have we seen it in mining? No, we have seen U.S. capital cutting back, retrenching, causing lay-offs in Labrador City and the whole of the Quebec north shore. There are colleagues of mine on the other side of the House as well as on this side, including the Prime Minister, who know that the record of U.S. capital has been one of retenchment, cutting back and the creation of unemployment. So the record is not good so far.
The Government's proposal, I presume, will be, in terms of my own province, that these new jobs will arrive as a result of the offshore agreement. The Government's response will probably be that it will create jobs in Newfoundland in that way. But we know too little about that because we do not know what is going to be in that offshore agreement. All we know is what the Prime Minister, when he was Leader of the Opposition, said in a letter to the Premier of Newfoundland. We have asked questions but we cannot get answers. We expect that there will probably be up front a development fund for Newfoundland of close to $500 million. A lot of money, but the question is: Will it be new money or simply recycled old money? That is the question I think we have to ask. Is it simply a redirection and recycling of the funds we along with the other Atlantic provinces have been used to receiving over the years as our fair share for regional industrial expansion. Every year P.E.I., for example, has received certain development funds from the Government of Canada, as has Newfoundland. But the point that should be made is that this money must be over and above that. I have asked the question but I have not got an answer.
How will this money be spent? Will it be spent on highways? Is this the money the Premier is going to use to wage his election in April when that offshore agreement is signed? Will there be an election and will this money be used for that? Will it build the highways? Will it be used to continue the trans-
Investment Canada Act
Labrador highway? These are the questions we have asked and to which we have not got answers. How much investment will there be in this offshore deal? Where will it come from? What will the return be to investors? What will the return be to the Government of Canada and the Government of Newfoundland? Who will set the royalties for Newfoundland? Will it be the Government of Canada or the Government of Newfoundland? How much will those royalties be? Apart from the initial fund we are going to get of $500 million, how much money are we going to get in my province and how soon?

Mr. Speaker, I know the Chair will be as generous with me and that I will certainly be entitled to an additional 15 seconds, as will other Members of the House. The generosity of the present occupant of the Chair is well known in this House.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, it does give me some pleasure to get up this afternoon and outlines some of my concerns about this matter. I think probably this is the first situation in which the present Government has imposed that nefarious provision of time allocation in limiting debate, that harsh measure which prohibits the democratic process of debate in this House. Many, many times I have heard the Conservatives in opposition stand up and bemoan the indignity and insufferable contempt of the democratic process which the Liberal Government's frequent use of closure demonstrated to this House. Now we have the Conservative Party imposing the same thing, breaking its electoral promises, breaking its commitment to Parliament to allow openness and fairness in government. If this was the only time that the Government went back on its promises, then maybe we could understand it. Maybe there is something we have missed in this Bill. Maybe there is in it such a tremendous imperative to Canada and Canadian needs that it demands our being sold down the river to the Americans. Maybe we missed it, but I do not think so.
The Conservative Party has now learned that it does not want open government. It has its program, its agenda, and closure will be the order of the day. It would have been nice, Mr. Speaker, if we could have established some type of relationship where we could have discussed these matters even more informally outside the Chamber. But that is not the way of the Conservative Party or of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) and his team of apparatchiks who are setting the agenda. They have laid out the scheme for the next five years and it is a shame.
I recall an incident earlier this week in the House which illustrates the kind of thing I am talking about. The treaty on salmon intervention between Canada and the United States is an example of the kind of contempt for the House of Com-

January 29, 1985
Investment Canada Act
mons and the people of Canada that this Government has which is illustrated by the closure motion today. You will know, of course, that in former years there has been an attempt to gain an interception treaty with the United States. The Prime Minister and his Cabinet approved this treaty with an undignified haste, and it has to be pointed out that it was done so against the wishes of many people who live on the coast of British Columbia and earn a living from fishing. They approved this treaty before they gave anyone documents relating to this particular agreement. The people of Canada and their elected representatives in the House of Commons were given the document after the Cabinet had ratified it. When the overseer, the former Liberal Minister of Finance and the grey eminence of the Liberal Party, Mitchell Sharp, came before the committee, he said that he did not really think anyone should be talking about this particular treaty lest the Americans not buy it. Frankly, I think we have given the Americans such a deal that their tongues will be hanging out to buy this particular treaty.
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, the way in which that treaty came into play makes me think that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) is just an errand boy for the Deputy Prime Minister and that team of apparatchiks that is running the Government, setting its priorities and issuing the marching orders. That treaty is not the kind of thing that the present Minister of Fisheries would be responsible for. That is not the kind of thing that he promised to the people of the area of this country whom he represents. The only way he would have done that is if the Deputy Prime Minister said, "You are going to do this because we have decided what is going to happen to the people in British Columbia". In fact, Mr. Speaker, the Deputy Prime Minister, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), and the priorities group were more interested in having something to give away to the President of the United States when he arrives in Quebec City than in protecting the interests of the people on the coast of British Columbia who depend on that fishing industry.
The Conservative Party formed a Government with probably the largest majority in Canadian history. It did so because of the many promises that the Prime Minister and the Members of the Party which is now governing the country made to people from one end of Canada to the other. It is ironic that many of the supporters of that Party who own tourist resorts in British Columbia are absolutely appalled at the treaty. They had been struggling to have meetings with the Minister and to have the issue brought before committee to have it studied before it was approved.
Many of those people have now been stabbed in the back by the Government. Enormous numbers of telegrams arrived on my desk yesterday and today from people concerned about what this will do to tourism in that area and to their businesses. They have had an example of this already. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans is now saying, "I will take total responsibility for what happens. We are not going to re-open this treaty. This is a fait accompli. We want it, we are going to
have it, and the Deputy Prime Minister has told me to do it". I think that is the case, Mr. Speaker.
The fishing industry is a good example of the contempt that is being demonstrated in the House today through this closure motion. When the present Minister of Fisheries and Oceans was supporting Conservative candidates along the coast of British Columbia, including the candidate in my riding, he talked about a fair buy-back program and about restructuring the fishing fleet in British Columbia in a meaningful way so as to respond to the traditional needs of the people in the industry and the small communities along the coast of British Columbia. Everyone recognized the need for restructuring and realigning that industry, but there were a lot of people who wanted the Government to recognize the traditional nature of that industry.
The documents that the Minister put before his advisory committee indicate that they are going to buy the banks' position. The banks will wind up being paid off. Everyone here recalls that the banks went through a period of lending enormous amounts of money to fishermen to buy new vessels and new technology to keep up with the industry on the West Coast. As the Government allowed interest rates to rise, many of these people found themselves in great financial difficulty. The banks found themselves with many loans which could not be paid off.
The present Minister intends to bail out those banks. Fishermen are going to lose their vessels. Communities along the coast of British Columbia are going to lose thousands of jobs. Many businesses such as ship repair operations in those communities are going to shut down. I think that even Members of the House of Commons will be directly affected by the way in which this industry is going to shrink on the coast of British Columbia because of the way in which the Minister is going to restructure this fleet and promote a buy-back program to bail out the banks. We are going to lose thousands of jobs and we are going to lose businesses. The traditional approach to fishing which people have enjoyed for many years is going to change dramatically on the coast of British Columbia.
This Minister has his marching orders from the Deputy Prime Minister and his apparatchiks who said, "Never mind what you or the Members of the Conservative Party who represent that area would like to do, we have the solution in mind to stop this problem". The present Minister of Fisheries and Oceans is on the coast of British Columbia right now selling British Columbians down the river in order to bail out the banks. He is going to make fishermen pay $200 million to the federal Government to promote a $100 million buy-back program. The federal Government is going to sell $100 million worth of vessels for $40 million. In short, through this buyback program, for which the fishermen must pay, the Government is going to make a neat profit of $160 million. It is going to bail out the banks, lose several thousand jobs on the coast of British Columbia, close down businesses, and change the traditional way of life along the coast. It is going to sell out the fishing industry to the Americans and put that business in serious difficulty.
