speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is the House ready for the question?

Mr. Speaker, this is the third time I have had an opportunity to speak in the debate on Bill C-15, and at this point, we must ask ourselves why this Government decided to move the previous question in connection with this Bill, a motion that will have the effect of blocking any further motions by the Opposition on second reading, thus in fact closing the debate on second reading on Bill C-15.
The question is particularly relevant since there is nothing of any substance on the Order Paper of the House of Commons. There is no important legislation that this Parliament would have to consider after the debate on Bill C-15. Sometimes I wonder whether the Opposition is not doing a favour to this Government that has been in power in September 4 of last year. Parliament has been in session since last fall, and since then no important legislation has been tabled. This from a party that claimed, when it was campaigning in Quebec and across Canada, that it had the answers to all Canada's problems. On the subject of employment, they said they were going to create hundreds of thousands of jobs as soon as the Government was sworn in, and now we see that during the months they have been in power, there has been less job creation than during the first three months Prime Minister Trudeau was in office and, on a monthly basis, fewer jobs than during the two months when the present Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) was Prime Minister of this country.
We might expect a political party that has been in the opposition for a number of years to come to power with specific solutions and draft legislation and policies, but all we get is blue, yellow, green or white papers setting up endless consultations. This is a Government that had no policy and no specific programs to put before the Canadian people.
It is indeed surprising that with its comfortable majority of 211 to 70, this Government should impose closure. Its slogans are consultation and dialogue, but it will not let Opposition Members, even though their numbers are relatively small, debate the only worthwhile Bill before the House. One wonders why they want to put the previous question at this time and why they want to choke off debate on Bill C-15. There are a number of possibilities, but it is a fact that since last fall, the Progressive Conservative Government has tried to make Canadians believe that because of the Foreign Investment Review Act there have been no substantial trade relations between Canada and the United States. As this debate continues it is becoming increasingly clear that the Prime Minister's speech in New York was entirely out of touch with reality.
Investment Canada Act
To prove this I would like to refer to a very interesting article by Michel Vastel in Actualite, which gives some revealing figures on the trade relations that exist between Canada and the United States and clearly demonstrates that the statements made by the Prime Minister of Canada in his New York speech did not reflect the actual situation. If we consider his statement that Canada is now open for business, I suggest we consider as well the figures quoted by Mr. Vastel in his article. He said that the Americans buy 72 per cent of our forestry products, 65 per cent of our petrochemical exports, 59 per cent of our metal production and nine-tenths of our energy exports including gas, oil and electric power. Conversely, Mr. Vastel goes on, Canadians purchase three-quarters of all their industrial imports from the United States. Thanks to the Automobile Pact, Americans provide 89 per cent of our car and spare parts imports, while 98 per cent of Canadian automobile production goes to the United States. Canada-U.S. trade is worth $35 billion more than trade between the United States and Japan. Mr. Vastel concludes that Canada is the United States' most important customer and that Ontario alone trades more intensively with the United States than does Japan. How could the Prime Minister of Canada say in his New York speech that now the Progressive Conservatives are in power, Canada is open for business, unless he was trying to deceive public opinion or send a message that went well beyond Bill C-15?
Mr. Speaker, in speaking to Bill C-15 on second reading, I have indicated these contradictions between the Government's rhetoric and the proposed Bill. I have the impression that this Government is putting the previous question because as Canadians are becoming better informed, they realize that Bill C-15 might have a disastrous effect on the Canadian economy and Canada's autonomy, not only vis-a-vis the United States but also internationally. They realize it may be wise to think twice before passing these measures. We on this side of the House intend to propose, at the committee stage, a number of significant amendments to this Bill to reflect these views. We would have preferred to propose a number of amendments to the principle of the Bill at the second reading stage, but the previous question, which has gagged the Opposition, has prevented us from doing so.
Mr. Speaker, were it not for the previous question, perhaps we would have had a chance to hear some of the backbenchers speak to this important legislation. I would very much like to know what some of the Members from Quebec think about this Bill. During the election campaign, they were making very emphatic speeches and asking their government to intervene to protect Canadian jobs, especially where the multinationals were concerned. I understand why some Hon. Members must be frustrated. On the other hand, I was not surprised

January 29, 1985
Investment Canada Act
to read letters in the newspapers, which referred to this Government as a "gouvernement de deux de pique", a term readily understood by those familiar with the French language, especially with expressions peculiar to certain regions in Quebec.
But instead of writing letters, those Members ought to take the floor in the Elouse and say exactly what they think, for perhaps some jobs in their ridings are likely to disappear if there is no longer any review of new investments. These might be in direct competition with Canadian companies operating in the various regions and creating jobs. Those companies might find it impossible to stand up against unfair competition on the part of investors anxious to compete on their own turf.
The central issue here is nothing more than the old debate on the national policy of the founder of the Conservatives and that reference to Canada's national policy. As you know, Mr. Speaker, there is logic in everything. Here we have Bill C-15, this open invitation to the Americans, and we hear various remarks about free trade zones, even though the words have yet to be defined. I can hardly wait to see the contents of the document which the Minister for International Trade is expected to make public this afternoon. I would have liked the Minister to table it in the House, but apparently it will be made public outside the House. All those pieces are part of a puzzle, and the Government wants us to pass Bill C-15 without showing us the other pieces of the puzzle.
I see that my time has expired, Mr. Speaker, and I thank you for your attention. I do hope that Government Members realize that the closure motion they are forcing upon us today flies in the face of every speech they made inside or outside the House.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have a few minutes before one o'clock and some time after Question Period to make some comments regarding the muzzling motion brought in by the Government. I presume that the Government does not want the Canadian public to know too much about Bill C-15.
Rather than talk about the problems created for Parliament as a result of closure motions such as this, I want to alert Canadians once again to the problems with Bill C-15 and why the Investment Canada Bill should be hoisted and sent back for redrafting. Although the Minister responsible for the Bill wants Canadians to think that this provides a new means for cutting red tape and eliminating the hindrances to the investment needed to create jobs in Canada, the facts are clear about what FIRA did. The Foreign Investment Review Act was a toothless monster and did not really do anything in the interest of Canada. I believe we should have a much tougher FIRA Bill than what the Government now proposes.
It is interesting to note that few government Members are getting up to applaud the benefits of Bill C-15. I believe that many of them, including yourself, Mr. Speaker, will probably notice that there are some tremendous flaws in Bill C-15.
Let me deal with some of the problems in terms of foreign investment coming to Canada to buy corporations or buy land and become involved in speculation. The first problem that was identified is that foreign-controlled companies do not spend nearly as much as Canadian-controlled companies on research and development, which is the key source of economic growth and productivity increase.
Let us look at some examples taken from studies by the Economic Council of Canada in 1983 and the Science Council of Canada in 1984. With respect to research and development, Canadian companies with less than 50 employees spent 11.2 per cent of their capital on R and D while foreign companies spent only 3.3 per cent. Canadian companies with 50 to 100 employees spent 10.1 per cent on R and D while foreign companies were still at only 4.3 per cent. Canadian firms with 100 to 200 employees dropped R and D spending to 9.1 per cent while such spending by foreign controlled companies plummetted down to 3.7 per cent. Of those corporations with more than 500 employees, Canadian companies spent 10.3 per cent on research and development while foreign companies spent a measly 2 per cent.
It becomes quite clear where the larger corporations, particularly foreign-owned corporations, conduct their research and development, which is one of the most important processes within our economy for the creation of new jobs. Those jobs occur outside the country, principally in the United States. I will expand on that at three o'clock, with your permission, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, the proposals dealing with the universality of social programs announced yesterday by the government are entirely unacceptable. For example, the reduction in family allowances considerably affects two groups already facing financial problems: women at home as well as families with low and medium incomes.
January 29, 1985

1 would like to state a few facts. Family allowance cheques are too often the only money paid to women at home. Families with low and medium incomes are affected by this government measure. Families with less than $10,000 a year receive less social benefits than those with $50,000 a year.
Where are the fine promises of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who wanted to tax bankers with $500,000 incomes? With such a reform, those people will still travel in a limousine paid with the money which in all fairness should be redistributed to the most needy.

Mr. Speaker, tax reform can be just only if we distinguish between tax deductions and tax exemptions.
A tax deduction is something optional. It may be given or taken away according to government policy. A tax exemption is essentially different. It is not optional. It recognizes there are parts of a person's income that do not come under the authority of the state.
The child tax exemption is a good example. It should not be seen as a benefit conferred by the state. It should be respected as a right. If parents have a natural duty to support their children, parents have a natural right to the income they need to give that support. That income should be exempt from the tax collector by right.
I speak of this because it is one difference between a socialist philosophy of taxation and a conservative one. Socialists presuppose the state has a right to take whatever part of a person's income it chooses to take. Whatever a person is left to enjoy he has simply by a decision of the state. A conservative philosophy of taxation says: "No. There are parts of a person's life that belong to him or her", and a person has a right to say to the tax collector: "No trespassing. Keep out. This is mine".

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Conservative Members, the Hon. Member for Champlain (Mr. Champagne), and the Hon. Member for Duvernay (Mr. Della Noce), for joining me and the NDP in speaking out for the ordinary Canadian consumer of gasoline who, frankly, is being hosed by the big oil companies of this country and tax greedy provincial and federal Governments. There is lots of talk about having independent Members of Parliament and Members of Parliament speaking out. When they do that, I think the media and the public should support them.
I have two down and 209 to go, Mr. Speaker. I tell the other 209 Conservative Members of Parliament to look at the report
today from Imperial Oil. It just announced its profits were up from $332 million to $533 million.
Paul Joseph from Burns Fry, energy consultants, expects Imperial's profit will be even higher in 1985. Imperial Oil is 69.5 per cent owned by Exxon of New York. What other country in the world would allow its major oil company to be foreign-owned, then give it tax breaks and so on to transfer money from ordinary Canadians at the pump to the oil company so it can buy more assets in Canada? Already the industry gets 52 per cent of the pie, or $11.6 billion, it wants more, and this Government is prepared to give more. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, that is more of the same.

It need not be that way. We once had a national dream, and we can have a dream again in which the ordinary Canadian consumer can have a break, and the big oil companies and tax-greedy provincial Governments will not benefit.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to bring to the attention of this House the concerns expressed to me by many of my constituents as a result of the recent propaganda film on abortion entitled "Abortion: Stories North and South".
The National Film Board provided funding for this film to pro-abortionist Gail Singer to present her one-sided view of this matter, which she had the audacity to call enlightening.
The only way to describe the misuse of public funds by the National Film Board to promote the pro-abortion view is outrageous. This abuse of public funds and trust cannot be tolerated.
I, as well as many other Canadians, believe that life begins at the moment of conception, and from this moment on the unborn are entitled to the same rights and privileges as we enjoy.
It is my opinion that we must stop using buzz words, such as "termination of pregnancy", and recognize abortion for what it really is, the murder of an unborn child.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to express my disappointment with respect to the proposed changes to the family allowances and the other child benefits provided to families.

January 29, 1985
The paper outlines two options which are in fact disguised as income tax increases for the middle class, without any substantial benefit for low income families. The Conservatives once said that they were aiming at the bank president, but they are hitting his janitor.
According to Option 1, families with an income lower than $10,000 would receive only 98 cents more per day, and families earning between $10,000 and $20,000, would have an increase of only 68 cents.
Option 2 is still worse. Families with an income lower than $10,000 would only get 48 cents more per day, and those earning between $10,000 and $20,000, 36 cents per day.
Moreover, the paper refers to family income, while in our Canadian tax system, the concept of family income is not recognized for general taxation purposes.
This means that if the Canadian government wants to implement either one of the two options outlined in the program tabled yesterday, surveys will have to be made covering a large number of families. After much dilly-dallying, this is all the Government could come up with. Quite simply, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has lost the battle he himself has started.
The Government is trying to hide the Minister of Finance's loss of credibility with some kind of cosmetic change that brings in significant tax increases for the middle class, but no substantial benefit for lower income families.

subtopic: CITY OF MONTREAL-HORNER COMMITTEE-BOMBARDIER CORPORATION PROPOSALS
CITY OF MONTREAL-HORNER COMMITTEE-BOMBARDIER CORPORATION PROPOSALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week, the city of Montreal, COPEM, the Cham-bre de commerce and the Montreal Board of Trade endorsed and submitted to the Horner Committee the Bombardier Corporation proposals. I agree with them that Montreal should be a transportation centre of Canada and that the policy of governments should be to contract work out to the private sector rather than leaving this field of endeavour to the responsibility of the public sector. However, I do not understand how they could have overlooked other Montreal companies, such as versatile Vickers in my constituency, which has been in operation for 74 years, which built the first subway in Montreal and which already has, which is not the case of Bombardier, the facilities needed to build and repair passenger cars, its physical plant extending over 205,000 square feet with a working capacity for more than 500 workers. This company has the equipment, the expertise and the technology required.
I would therefore like to ask the City of Montreal to reconsider its position and the Horner Committee to take these facts into account. One of its members should not be favoured to the disadvantage of others, especially since Bombardier has joined with the Urban Transport Development Corporation to put in tenders for the contracts of the Federal Government and Ontario to build new trains for VIA Rail. Maintenance could perhaps be left to another company.

subtopic: SASKATCHEWAN BREAD PRICE WAR-IMPACT ON SMALL BAKERIES
SASKATCHEWAN BREAD PRICE WAR-IMPACT ON SMALL BAKERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, due to a price war on bread which is currently raging in Saskatchewan between the two major suppliers, Westons and McGavins, smaller bakeries across the province are being forced out of business. I have had appeals from many small bakeries requesting that action be taken on their behalf so that they will not go under as a result of excessive price cutting.
Their complaints are fully justified. These are important small business people who are major contributors to the wellbeing of local economies. If they do not survive this price war, the unemployment lines will continue to grow even longer, and bread prices will quickly rise to above the old price level as soon as the local bakeries are out of business.
Bread which has been sold at $1.05 a loaf retail will not remain at the 58-cent a loaf retail currently in place. Once the small bakeries are pushed out and McGavins and Westons take over, $1.05 will look cheap by comparison.
I urge the Government to take immediate action through the Combines Investigation Act so that these small businesses can continue to remain open. This will provide customers with a choice, and will allow local bakeries to continue to play an important role in their local economy. Surely a Government which claims to be open for business cannot stand idly by while giants in the bread industry shut down small bakeries in their bid for total control of the bread market.

Mr. Speaker, last year was a tragic one for India. We saw the assassination of Prime Minister Gandhi and large scale communal violence in the events leading up to and following her assassination. These and other events in India have seen Indian pitted against Indian, and sometimes members of one religion have attacked members of another religion solely because of religion. Other events, such as the recent tragedy in Bhopal, have
January 29, 1985

cut across religions. These events have, to some extent, spilled over into Canada. Relations between Canadians with Indian backgrounds of different religions have sometimes become strained.
That is why last month, in Toronto, a group of Canadians, primarily of Indian background from the major religions in India, formed the Indo-Canadian Assistance Society. This non-profit society was formed to aid victims of communal violence in India regardless of religion, as well as to aid victims of the recent chemical accident in Bhopal. The president is Christin, the treasurer is Hindu, the secretary is Sikh, and the first vice-president is Moslem.
Already two Members in addition to myself, the Member for Dollard (Mr. Weiner) and the Member for Edmonton Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour), have agreed to become honorary presidents of the Society. Hopefully all of us can work together to bring aid to those suffering in India and, by working together in Canada, ensure that religious differences between Canadians are minimized.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT INITIATIVES SOUGHT TO ASSIST GLACE BAY, N.S.
GOVERNMENT INITIATIVES SOUGHT TO ASSIST GLACE BAY, N.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as most Members are aware, the town of Glace Bay and the surrounding areas suffered another serious economic setback this past Saturday due to a fire which destroyed the Highland Fisheries fish plant, throwing another 350 persons out of work. This is the second economic blow within a year to a community which was devastated by the fire at the No. 26 Colliery, leaving 1,200 miners unemployed. The unemployment rate has now soared to 55 per cent.
As I was meeting with town officials and the owner of the fish plant yesterday to discuss the situation, I was unable to be present in the House yesterday, but was heartened by the assurance of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) to assist the town with whatever the Government can do.
There are many initiatives which the Government can take. It is this Minister who has the responsibility to move on them. First, the Government could sign a federal-provincial subsidiary agreement on infrastructure projects for the town of Glace Bay. Second, it could initiate a pre-retirement plan for older miners, thus enabling the younger ones to obtain jobs and plan for the future. Third, it could make a firm commitment on new coal developments for the town of Glace Bay. I urge the Minister to take action forthwith.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday in Montreal the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association inaugurated its 72nd annual meeting. The Canadian industry is feeling somewhat optimistic and is looking forward to increasing its production to 68 million tons by 1995. To achieve that goal, the industry is ready to invest from $3 to $5 billion per year to update its pulp and paper facilities to bring about an era of increased productivity, more competitive prices and wider profit margin. It should be emphasized that 1984 witnessed an increase of 6.2 per cent in production over the previous year.
Here is the case of a thriving industry, thanks to the consultations and agreements we have had with the provinces in the area of forest husbandry. We believe in the future of the forest industry in Canada in general and of the pulp and paper industry in particular, and we want to demonstrate our support and commitment to the industrial corporations and associations which are helping in the recovery of our country.

subtopic: ACID RAIN-CALL FOR REDUCTION IN AUTOMOBILE EMISSIONS
ACID RAIN-CALL FOR REDUCTION IN AUTOMOBILE EMISSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) has indicated that the approach of the Government with respect to acid rain from here on in will be to emphasize the bilateral nature of the problem as opposed to the international nature. I suggest to the Minister that while she should continue to emphasize the international aspect of it, with respect to the bilateral relationships on acid rain, and particularly with respect to the United States, she should do two things.
First, she should really restore the Herring Gull egg program to show that we are concerned about the environment. We could then be appropriately self-righteous with the United States when it comes to the environment. Second, she could ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) to bring in reduced auto emissions immediately, which also have to do with acid rain. Then, when we approach the United States with respect to acid rain, we will have cleaned up our own back yard, first on the wider environmental issue of Great Lakes water quality and, second, with respect to auto emissions. The Minister of Transport should do something now about that.

subtopic: TAX EXEMPTION FOR FAMILIES WITH CHILDREN- GOVERNMENT POSITION
TAX EXEMPTION FOR FAMILIES WITH CHILDREN- GOVERNMENT POSITION

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Stevens that Bill C-15, an Act respecting investment in Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Regional Development: and on the motion of Mrs. Tardif (Charlesbourg) (p. 1708).

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to resume debate from before the lunch break with regard to the muzzling order that has been brought in by the Government with respect to the so-called Investment Canada Bill.
In resuming my remarks this afternoon, let me touch on the key points of which I think Canadians are aware but which they do not often think about in relation to the new legislation

January 29, 1985
Investment Canada Act
that was introduced by the Minister. Let me go through some of the features of the old Foreign Investment Review Act and cite questions which would be asked of major foreign takeovers, according to the Act.
The first question is if it will provide jobs for Canadians. I suggest that this is a very appropriate question to ask about foreign capital coming into Canada. One can only wonder why the new Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) would not want that test to apply.
Another question is, will it improve Canada's export performance? Again, one would assume that such a test is one that ought to apply to foreign capital coming into the country. Will it contribute to having more of Canada's raw material processed within our own borders? I suggest that that is a test spoken about frequently by all political Parties during federal elections but one which seems to have been bypassed by this new legislation.
Will the applicant provide new investment within Canada? I believe that question is inherent in any foreign investment, whether we are talking about the old Bill or the new Bill.
Will the applicant buy supplies in Canada, provided they are competitively priced? I intend to expand on that point in a few moments. A key consideration for a foreign enterprise coming into Canada is where it buys its inventory and raw materials. That is crucially important.
Will there be new opportunities for Canadians to be shareholders, directors and managers of the enterprise? That is a crucially important test in order to determine if Canadians will have an opportunity to give direction to a corporate entity without provincial or federal government involvement so that the enterprise will operate in the direction in which the country wants to go.
Will it improve Canada's access to new products and processes? One would hope that that kind of test could stay within the legislation, but again we see that the new Minister has removed it. Will it improve Canada's industrial productivity? One would hope that that test would be applied, but the Tories have decided that it is inappropriate.
Will it increase the level of competition? Surely one would hope that the opposite would not be the case and, therefore, one must ask why the Conservatives would want to remove such a test from a Bill related to foreign investment.
Is it compatible with the Government's industrial and economic policies? That seems to be a basic and fundamental test that is applied in every industrial country around the world, whether democratic or not. One would expect that test to be applied.
Let me expand on the shortcomings of this Bill. Even the Toronto Star on December 9, 1984, described the foreign investment proposals of the new Government as being "Stevens' shortsighted gamble". The article states:
The danger in Stevens' approach, consequently, is that it risks long-term pain for short-term gain. If he does succeed in attracting an influx of new branch plant operations without any requirement that they operate in Canada's best
interests, we may see some short-term increase in jobs-but what will our economy look like 10 years from now?
The peril is that we could end up with an economy with an even higher degree of foreign ownership than at present, a diminished capacity both to export and to innovate and hence to make our own way in an increasingly competitive world- and therefore, in the long run, with fewer opportunities to create good jobs for Canadians.
I think a few facts are important in this debate even though we could spend the brief time that we have discussing why closure on this Bill is so inappropriate. I think it is important to raise some facts about why this legislation should be redrafted. Despite the FIRA approval rate over the past two years, which was up between 95 per cent and 98 per cent, less than one-half of those approved foreign takeovers intended to increase investment or provide any new jobs. Since the beginning of 1984, 15 per cent of those approved promised neither new jobs nor new investment. It was simply a case of a big fish eating a Canadian fish.
Second, Canada has more foreign ownership and control per capita than any other industrialized nation in the world and more than many developing countries.
Third, Canada imports more duty-free, finished manufacturing goods, even excluding automotive goods, than do the United States, Japan and the European Economic Community combined. That fact comes from the Science Council of Canada.
According to Canadian Business, of the top 50 companies in Canada, the greatest number of lost jobs over the past few years has been from U.S.-owned companies.
In 1983, Canada had a deficit of S9.4 billion in interest and dividend payments. Since the record was begun in 1926, Canada has been a net exporter of interest and dividend funds.
Foreign investors used Canadian found capital to further expand and take over inside Canada. That has been demonstrated time and again. Foreign capital comes in and acquires either a branch plant or a mine within Canada and then uses our money, banking and credit union system to buy up more and channel more dividends and profits to the foreign country.
Foreign corporations take resources home to create jobs in manufacturing in the parent country. I gave some statistics with respect to that this morning. The amount of resources that are distributed back out of Canada to the parent country is devastating. Seventy-two per cent of all imports into Canada were designated for foreign-controlled firms, which deteriorates our balance of payments. That fact comes from a Statistics Canada study in 1978.
Canada's trade deficit in end products was $14.9 billion in 1983 and, to the end of October, 1984, it stands at $15.5 billion.
According to the U.S. Senate committee, in 1981, "Much of our trade with foreign countries originates with orders placed by subsidiaries of U.S. companies located overseas. For example, 75 per cent of our exports to the 300 largest companies in Canada originates from the subsidiaries of U.S. firms".
I am pleased to have had a chance to say a few words on this Bill that is in dire need of redrafting.
January 29, 1985

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on the specific motion of closure. I believe as a Member of Parliament that I have a responsibility to indicate to my constituents who elected me on September 4 where I stand on issues. I believe it is the obligation of each and every Member of this House to do that so that their constituents may determine how a Member feels about issues of concern to the nation.
1 note with respect to this particular Bill that very few government Members have spoken. There are 211 government Members, yet only a handful have deemed it necessary to express their points of view. It seems to me that either Members do not care, they have nothing to say, or they were instructed not to speak. I suspect the latter is the case. I suspect that the House Leader or the powers that be in the Conservative Party have advised Members not to speak on this Bill in order to have the Bill become law as quickly as possible.
It is interesting to note that a special parliamentary committee has been established to investigate the role of the backbencher in order to advise Parliament and the Government on how the role of the back-bencher can be enhanced. It seems somewhat hypocritical of the Government to embark on this parliamentary investigation while, on the other hand, effectively muzzling Government Members from speaking.
I submit, your honour, that government Members as well as opposition Members do a very serious disservice to their constituents by not standing up to express their points of view and give Canadians some insight and information on why they support or do not support the particular piece of legislation before the House. I concede that it may be important for government Members to support the legislation because it is a government initiative, but that does not stop Members from standing up in this House to explain why they support a particular Bill. Once again, it is my respectful submission that constituents, and Canadians as a whole, have to know where a particular Member stands.
The Government talks about enhancing the role of the back-bencher. How hypocritical. One recognizes that the opportunities for a government back-bencher are somewhat limited. Opportunities to ask questions during Question Period are limited and, because of the sheer numbers, opportunities are limited with respect to Standing Order 21 statements, and with respect to contributions to deliberations of standing committees of this Parliament opportunities are limited. Yet here is an opportunity for government Members to stand up and say, "I support the Bill for the following reasons," or, "I do not support the Bill for the following reasons," or, "I am suggesting possible amendments or alternatives to this legislation".
I challenge government back-benchers to speak. By not doing so they are not doing an effective job. A farce is being made of this special parliamentary committee and its deliberations.
With respect to the motion before the House, I want to indicate my very serious concern and chagrin at the method by
Investment Canada Act
which this motion was introduced. As a result of parliamentary trickery, a Government back-bencher introduced this closure motion. It is my submission that the closure motion we are presently debating is an abuse. It is an absolute abuse of the majority which the Government holds in this House today.
Canadians were fearful after the reality of September 4 because of the lop-sided majority of this Parliament. Their fears are well founded, Mr. Speaker. In my view this is but the beginning of how this Government intends to abuse the overwhelming majority it has.
The Government, by introducing this motion, is effectively denying any further opportunity for any more substantive motions. It is unhealthy for a democratic system that the Government in its wisdom has decided to introduce this amendment. The Opposition, as is obvious, has some very serious concerns with respect to this legislation. It is a major piece of legislation. It is the Government's first major piece of legislation. It seems to me that it is incumbent upon the Government to ensure that a full and complete debate occurs on this legislation because it is serious and important and it will affect Canadians from coast to coast.
This is a marked departure from the policies of the previous administration. It is a departure from the way we deal with foreign investment. On that basis, the Government is obligated, not only by the huge majority it holds but also by respect for Parliament and respect for this House, to ensure that a full debate occurs.
This Government has decided to invoke this form of closure. I concede that the Opposition will have other opportunities to express its point of view on this Bill. The Bill will go to committee and the Opposition will have the opportunity to speak at committee and to introduce amendments considered necessary and advisable in the best interests of Canadians.
This Government has set a very dangerous precedent for the remainder of this Parliament by deciding to invoke closure. It is but the beginning. I pray that the Government recognizes the importance of respect for Parliament, for the right of the minority, the right of both minority Parties, to be heard. By invoking this drastic measure of closure, this Government, in my respectful opinion, has shown disrespect for this Parliament and disrespect for the traditions of Parliament.
It seems to me that nothing would be lost except a few precious weeks or months if the Government were to allow the Opposition to have a full debate. It appears that this Government is bent on ramming this legislation through without consideration. It claims that it is a consultative government. During Question Period today, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) indicated they wanted to consult with respect to social programs, that they wanted Canadians to have input with respect to these major changes. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, where was the input with respect to this piece of legislation? With whom did the Government consult other than the rich boys on Bay Street and the oil barons in Calgary? What about others? Were others consulted? Were options put forward as were the options concerning universality and social programs?

January 29, 1985
Investment Canada Act
Were options given to Canadians? The answer is a simple no. The Government decided there would be no option.
I recognize that my time for speaking has expired. I simply wish to reiterate my very serious concern with respect to the Government's actions to effectively end debate. In my respectful opinion, it does not bode well for the future workings of this Parliament and democracy per se.

Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that I have to speak on what in effect is a closure motion. It was interesting to listen to the last speaker, the representative of the Liberal Party, talking about how a closure motion hurts Parliament and how it is undemocratic. In your many years in the Opposition, Mr. Speaker, I am sure you remember that quite often various members of the Liberal Party introduced various forms of closure or motions to restrict the ability of the Opposition to debate and raise issues in the House of Commons. When the Liberals are on this side of the House they say one thing, but they say and do the exact opposite when they are in government.
The hypocrisy is not only to my right; it is also across the way. When you were in opposition, Mr. Speaker, you were joined by people who are now part of the Government Party who would rant and rave against motions of closure. For that matter, you probably remember an incident where the Conservative Members actually charged the Speaker on a matter of closure. I am not recommending that as a course of action to be taken, but it reminds us that when the Conservatives were on this side of the House they were completely opposed to any limitations on debate in the House of Commons.
I recognize that from time to time there is a need to limit debate in the House of Commons, but this is not one of those occasions. This Government came to power last fall. It did not introduce this Bill until December and it is now toward the end of January. We have had only a few days of debate on the Bill. Most of the country does not know what is in this legislation. One way that Members of the House of Commons have of getting information to the public is by making speeches in the House of Commons. The closure motion before us today means that within the next day or two debate will come to an end.
As a result of this legislation, we are again hearing about a group which had died two or three years ago, the Committee for an Independent Canada. As a result of the actions of this Government, this legislation in particular, that group is talking about re-emerging. Unfortunately, if we rush through the passage of the second reading of this legislation, send it to committee and the Government again forces closure at that stage, groups concerned about the economy and the ownership of the industries of our nation will not have a real opportunity to protest this legislation. That is a serious concern for all of us.
A number of speakers from the New Democratic Party stated that we in this nation have one of the highest percentages of industries owned by foreign people and corporations. Others from our caucus have pointed out that most of our natural resources are not owned by Canadians. Member after Member has given examples of where American owned firms have applied American law in their dealings rather than Canadian law.
I am glad to see the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) in the Chamber. He will know that on occasion firms operating in Canada have not followed the policy of this Government. They have followed the policy of the American Government or their home nation. Jobs are lost in Canada not because of Canadian policy but because of American policy.
I spoke on this legislation last week. I did not read quotes from labour movements, socialists or Canadian nationals. I did read some quotes from the Science Council of Canada, a government agency headed by a former leader of the Liberal Party for Ontario, Dr. Stuart Smith. I referred to a study done by Frank Longo for the Science Council of Canada on the history of research and development by foreign-owned firms in Canada in comparison to Canadian-owned firms. Mr. Longo's study found that by and large foreign-owned firms did less research and development in this nation than Canadian-owned firms. On average, therefore, a foreign-owned firm will do less research and development in Canada. I repeat, that study was done by the Science Council of Canada.
Even with the weak legislation that exists at the present time, we do not get the same amount of research and development from foreign-owned firms that we get from Canadian firms. For the Government at this time to look at further weakening those very limited controls on foreign investment will result in our having less control and less say about our future.
Mr. Longo's study also looked at what happened with money supplied by the Canadian Government with regard to foreign investors. It is interesting to note that Canadian firms by and large, though not everyone, took the money they received from government grants and matched it dollar for dollar in order to do research and development in this nation. Not so with foreign-owned firms. There were exceptions and some foreign-owned firms did a good job of research and development in this country, but on average they did not match and only used the federal Government supplied money. Not only do we have less research and development done by foreign-owned firms, but they do not even match the money they receive from the federal Government in order to do research.
I referred that study to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens). I have a letter here from the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion in which he admits that he does not know what study I am talking about. I referred to the author and that it was done by the Science Council of Canada. If a Minister has a study that affects legislation before this House, he should read that study. That study was paid for by the taxpayers of Canada. It looked at how our economy can be developed and the Minister has not even considered it.

I recognize that as a result of the closure motion before us, I have only one more minute to speak. I plead with the government back-benchers, the silent majority in this House of Commons, to consider their role in the House of Commons. Consider what will happen to research and development, what it will do to the opportunities for our young people, our opportunities for economic development in the future, and vote against this legislation. Members have a duty. I ask them to please carry out that duty for the benefit of their constituents.

Mr. Speaker, I join with my colleagues in participating in this debate. I must say at the outset that when I read the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Charlesbourg (Mrs. Tardif), I was quite surprised, particularly in view of the fact that the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) is present in the House. I can recall with great clarity that when he was on this side of the House, he vigorously opposed any limitations on debate which came before the floor of the House of Commons. I also recall, as I am sure you do, Mr. Speaker, that occasion one evening when Members of Parliament from the Conservative side rushed the Speaker's chair.
The limitations that are being put on the debate today, at a time when the whole substantive issue of foreign investment has not been thoroughly discussed by Members of Parliament in this Chamber, seems to me to be a bit unfair. It seems to me that the Government, very unwisely, is rushing its legislative timetable. When the Bill was initially tabled in the House of Commons, I thought it was a mistake. I would have thought that this Bill would have come forward after some consultation with the Canadian people and the Members of the House of Commons. After all, were we not told by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) that consultation would be the key, operative word for the new Government? Instead, we saw two incidents. One was an arbitrary cutting of $4.2 billion from the Canadian economy; the other was an attempt to pass a piece of legislation dealing with foreign investment without any meaningful consultation with Canadians. That seems to fly in the face of the arguments made so eloquently by Conservative Members that there ought to be consultation. Nevertheless, this piece of legislation is now before us.
I am a bit saddened to see that government Members, for whatever reasons-I can only assume they are good reasons- do not wish to join one after the other in debating the substantive portions of this particular Bill. To try to perpetrate this piece of legislation on the Canadian people in a limited amount of time flies in the face of what members of the Conservative Party did while they were in opposition.
Investment Canada Act
I think it is very distasteful that we as Members of Parliament, at a time when a committee has been appointed by the House to review the role of Members of Parliament, are now confronted with a piece of legislation which we must pass within a limited period of time. That is totally unacceptable, particularly if we are to change the way Parliament works and the way Parliament ought to work.
The substance of the Bill that is before us leaves a great deal to be desired both for Members of the House of Commons and, I am sure, for Members of the other place. Equally so, there are other legislatures across the country that have some grave concerns about the substantive parts of this Bill. I recall that the present Minister of Development for the Province of Nova Scotia, a member of the provincial Conservative Party, has expressed some serious doubts as to how far this Bill will go in terms of attracting investment, particularly to Nova Scotia. It is frustrating to see the Government trying to rush this Bill through very quickly, but it is even more frustrating to see that those of a different political stripe than I have legitimate concerns about this piece of legislation.
Second, Mr. Speaker, Canadians from all regions of the country are concerned that the lack of foreign investment review, which would be the pith and substance of the Bill, will allow for investment from abroad which has no regulatory control. I think Canadians in all regions of Canada are concerned about that. I would have thought that Members opposite would have wanted to have the opportunity to debate that matter on the floor of the House of Commons. Apparently the exact opposite is the case.
I was also disappointed that the Minister responsible, in speaking to the substance of this Bill, failed for whatever reasons to place before Parliament a document which would clearly spell out the jobs that he would anticipate as a result of the passing of this legislation. Members of Parliament were told that if this piece of legislation were to be passed, it would create wealth, jobs and prosperity. We were told it would open the doors and give our young people, women and minority groups an opportunity to have meaningful employment. I think all Members of Parliament would applaud that objective. However, the Government went a step farther; it indicated that that would happen forthwith.
All I have asked of the Minister and of his officials is to provide the documentation regarding jobs here on the floor of the House of Commons so that Members of Parliament who may have different ideologies, philosophies and approaches to the running of the economy can debate what those numbers mean. Unfortunately, the Minister responsible has not seen fit to comply with that very reasonable and objective request. I suggest that that would make one a little suspicious of the Government's intentions.
First we had a Government that talked about jobs, jobs, jobs. Then it talked about consultation, consultation, consultation. There have been no jobs. With regard to this piece of legislation, there has been no consultation and the Government is trying to slam it through. Time and time again, both in the House of Commons and through the news media, I have heard

Investment Canada Act

In fact, I find that what exist are fears, apprehensions and a suspicion of the Government's intention incoming forward with a document like Investment Canada so early in its mandate.
If one wished to be political, one would believe that there is a rift between the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens), and that one is trying to outdo the other. Perhaps the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion really wants to be the Minister of Finance and that is why he has jumped the gun on his colleague, the Minister of Finance. I hope there is no disunity on the other side because those on the other side have a major mandate to carry out for the Canadian people.
The changing of the Foreign Investment Review Act, as we know it today, to Investment Canada is not supported by any evidence put forward by the Conservative Party that states unequivocally that jobs will be created in each of the provinces of Canada. Job guarantees are very important. I have had experience with foreign investment. We welcome foreign investment, but there must be some restrictions on where that foreign investment goes and how it will operate within the Canadian economy. I suggest that the Prime Minister went to Washington prematurely. He went to New York and to Washington and gave them all that they requested without attempting to obtain reciprocity with regard to the things which we were seeking in Canada. I think that is a pretty immature way of running the country and improving the Canadian economy.
I hope that other Members will join in this debate and express their thoughts as to how we should proceed from here.

Mr. Speaker, I too wish to join in this debate which has imposed closure on Bill C-15. It is with sadness that I note it is the first motion of closure which has been introduced by the new Conservative Government. There is a little voice in the back of my head which suggests that it will not be the last which we will see. In fact, it is probably the first of many to come.
It is also sad that a Party which was so eloquent in opposition in denouncing the motions of closure which the former Liberal Government introduced, on numerous occasions and
many times for no justifiable reason, now committing exactly the same sin. It is amazing to see, in the men and women who sit across the aisle, the type of conversion and mind change which has occurred. Indeed, power corrupts. What amazes me is how soon and how quickly power corrupts.
It is also somewhat discouraging that so few government Members have risen to explain and justify this legislation. We have heard some very simplistic statements and slogans which government Members like to put forth. This legislation is essentially based on simplistic premises, the major one being that the problem which exists in Canada today is that there is not enough foreign investment. They say it is because those naughty Liberals were really socialists and closed the door to foreign investment, and that that is why we have an unemployment rage which is so high in Canada. So all we need do is open up the gates and foreign investment will come in and create the jobs and prosperity needed to put Canada back on the road to economic recovery.
I appreciate that Members in the House-who after all are politicians-give political speeches, and that often those speeches contain simplistic notions. What concerns me is that this is not just speech material but the actual policy and thinking of the present Government. It scares me, because if this is the policy it is simplistic, and it will not bring about the desired solutions. However, it will create more problems in the future.
First, I would like to deal with the notion that FIRA and the former Liberal Government which introduced and administered FIRA were made up of a bunch of socialists who stopped the flood of foreign investment. We could not get further from the truth. If we consider that 95 per cent to 98 per cent of the applications in the last two years were approved by the Liberal Government, we begin to realize that FIRA was indeed a toothless tiger. It did not hold back foreign investment. If we consider that Canada has more foreign ownership and control per capita than any other industrialized nation, we begin to realize that most of this occurred under previous Liberal Governments. So to make the charge that it was FIRA and the Liberals which stopped the flood of foreign investment does not make sense.
Second, the simplistic notion which has been put forward is: Let's get rid of FIRA and foreign investment will come into Canada. I suggest that that will not happen because in the past FIRA has not been effective and there are no great globs of foreign investment waiting to come into Canada after this legislation is passed. The Globe and Mail did some background checking with investors and bankers in the United States-mainly in New York-which showed that very few had any expectations of new investment flowing into Canada. I think the Tories are suffering some disillusionment. They believe that because they were elected and because they are bringing in this legislation, all of a sudden foreign investment will come into Canada. Foreign investment occurs when there are certain economic and social conditions; mainly the condition that there is a profit in the investment. Investors already have enough investment in Canada and see no reason to open
January 29, 1985

new branch plants. For the moment they have enough; there is no need for them to establish new centres of production in Canada.
Much of what we have heard during this debate is frivolous and has no basis in terms of reality. When we hear the odd Conservative spokesman say "Pass this legislation and new investment will come in", I believe it is a phoney statement. When we hear Liberal members stand up to proclaim the evils of foreign investment, that too is phoney. The fact that this country, on a per capita basis, is owned by more foreigners than any other developed country in the world is the result of the actions of Liberal Governments.
The simplistic idea that if we bring forth more foreign investment it will cure all our ills is dangerous. It can create on a short-term basis some jobs and development in Canada; there is no denying that. But people invest in something because they expect to get more out than they put in. Eventually, a day of reckoning must occur. The money going out, in terms of dividends and interest payments, is greater than the new investment money which is coming in.
The day of reckoning occurred in Canada some time ago. Canada has a greater outflow of capital in the form of dividend payments than it has in new capital coming in. Therefore, in order to cover our deficit in the balance of payments, we try to encourage more new capital to come in. It is like digging a hole in order to get the dirt to fill up the hole which was dug some time ago. But in the process a deeper hole has been dug. That means that the future must be mortgaged in order to service the debts of the present. The Conservatives have not given us a change in Canadian Government policy but a continuation of the policies which existed in previous Liberal Governments. It is an attempt to get more foreign capital to come into Canada in order to pay the deficit resulting from the flow of capital which is leaving the country. It is stupid economic policy and it will not work. We are only postponing serious problems with which future generations will be forced to deal.
There are numerous studies which show that foreign investment is not necessarily the solution to a country's problems. We have seen studies which suggest that research and development suffers when most of the country's major industries are branch plants of foreign multi-nationals. We have seen, in such an economy as we have in Canada, that the employment rate decreases when a vast majority of the plants are foreign-owned. We see that there is a negative outflow of capital funds. We see that the social, economic and political independence of a country gets eroded when a good hunk of its economy is foreign controlled.
Something I also find discouraging in the Government's economic policy is that it is one which is backward-looking. 1 had hoped that with the election of a new Government with new faces, some new outlooks would be introduced. We are moving into a new social and economic age. By all signs it seems that in this new age, production should be small scale,
Investment Canada Act
that there should be community, country and regional self-sufficiency, and that the new products coming on the market should be intensive in information and technology. It is customization versus mass production.
The indications are that this is the economy of the new age. The Bill which is in front of us ties us into an old age of mass production, world-wide mandates and into a type of economy which is owned by multi-nationals and controlled from outside our borders. The encouragement of this kind of economy is a sin.

Mr. Speaker, as I understand it, the Government's insistence on dismantling the Foreign Investment Review Agency is based on the premise that by doing so Canada would somehow manage to generate hundreds of thousands of jobs overnight, and that much of the problem of Canada's lack of productivity and high unemployment at present stems from the very fact of FIRAs existence. In my view, Mr. Speaker, the mismanagement of successive Liberal Governments is hardly a reason for blaming FIRA.
The experience of this country with FIRA is that it has not prevented foreign investment. The figures show quite the contrary. If FIRA can be blamed for anything, it is for perhaps being overly bureaucratic in its decision-making process and for unnecessarily delaying investment decisions by foreign investors. Certainly the figures clearly indicate that foreign investment in Canada has not declined to any degree at all since FIRA was established. I believe the figures show that 98 per cent of all applications to FIRA were approved. Therefore, to make an ideological argument that FIRA somehow destroys investment opportunities in Canada is seriously misleading the public.
If indeed the Government is making that kind of ideological decision because it does not like public agencies, that is something else, and the Government should come out and clearly say so. That would be better than saying that if we get rid of FIRA we can create all kinds of jobs overnight. I would like to see this Government come forward with some figures which would clearly indicate that. Perhaps if it did so Members of the Opposition might look more kindly up on what the Government is trying to do. However, Mr. Speaker, I can tell you from my own personal experience that FIRA, its decisionmaking process, and Government policy towards FIRA, have done nothing to protect Canadian workers or the Canadian market-place.
This is a serious situation, Mr. Speaker. For example, Canadian General Electric is a part of the branch plant economy and whether or not that corporation has provided a direct benefit to Canadians can be seriously questioned. In a plant in Toronto called the Radio Valve plant which later became the Canadian General Electric plant, the company was

involved in production of vacuum tubes for televisions and radios. That plant was closed by CGE around 1969. The argument was that it was no longer a viable operation. In fact, the company closed that plant as part of an international rationalization program. They decided that plant was not profitable for the purpose of continuing to supply the Canadian market with vacuum tubes for television sets. Perhaps they may have had an argument there, but they moved production of that plant to a plant in the United States and continued to import exactly the same product into the Canadian marketplace. In the process they threw 800 Canadians out of work. Some of those people had seniority with that company in excess of 40 years.
That, Mr. Speaker, is not the kind of investment that I or other Canadians want to see. Surely if we allow companies to come into Canada to exploit our market-place and Canadian workers in order to make a profit, then they have an obligation to prove they will make a significant contribution to Canada and Canadians. From my experience that has not taken place.
If you look at the major industries in our country, Mr. Speaker, you will find that most of them are dominated by foreign companies. I think it is also safe to say, and many people would agree with me because I have heard it expressed, that Canada is probably the only country in the world in the process of de-industrialization. Most countries are industrializing. One of the major reasons for that is the large degree of foreign control of investment in this country. We have no say at all about how that is controlled, and we had none even with FIRA. I predict it will be even worse once we get rid of FIRA and end up with this new agency the present Government wants to bring out.
I want to mention two other instances more current than that of Canadian General Electric which I spoke about. The first is the Black & Decker plant closure in Barrie, Ontario. That company received approval last year to buy into the CGE operation in Barrie, and less than a year after receiving approval they turned around and are now closing that plant to consolidate it with another operation of the company. They are now laying off some 500 workers, I believe.
That, too, is not the kind of investment we think this Government should be encouraging; or if it is going to encourage it, make sure that when that corporation establishes itself in the country it is not going to do the kind of things that Black & Decker is doing in Barrie, Ontario.

The results of the post-war decision to open up the country for investment by multi-national companies was clearly pointed out. By the middle 1960s we had essentially become a branch plant economy. While that is no longer so much the case, there is a branch plant economy still existing in some sectors. The implementation of the policy for investing in Canada forced a change in that existing attitude. Of course, that attitude was formed in part by the investment community and the manufacturing sector in Canada at that time.
I think one problem was that the existing institutions did not want to be threatened by other Canadian challenges. Therefore many companies did not issue shares for expansion purposes but chose to finance through banks, trust companies or insurance companies. As a result, there was a small club of the large investment community that was operating within itself. This prevented an opportunity for small investors to become a part of the over-all expansion of larger plants and industrial processes.
A recent example of this is Nova Corporation, which is essentially an Alberta-based corporation. That company came to Ottawa to explain its activities and talk about some government policies it had experienced in past years. I believe its comments are pertinent to this debate on the Investment Canada Bill as a result of which there will virtually be new rules regarding the importation of foreign capital into the country. Their comments also pertain to how the large investment community acts within itself.
Businessmen face difficulties when they attempt to build a company and attract investment by issuing new shares. This is the course which Nova Corporation chose to take but that company and others like it do so at some cost. If it issues new shares to accommodate the new investment, the value of its shares will remain relatively flat. It was competing in a market-place which chose to hold the same amount of shares and finance internally through the banks or trust companies rather than to issue new shares. Therefore the value of those shares would escalate quite quickly.
I remind the House that most of the investment funds in Canada are being held by insurance companies or trust companies. They tend to look for shares that have a history of increasing in value very rapidly on a consistent basis. That type of money is attracted to companies which are borrowing but not enlarging the shareholder base, not paying dividends or taxes. It is a combination of our tax policy and investment policy which has been determining the kind of new investment that takes place in the country.
A company like Nova Corporation which was attempting to expand by issuing new shares and new stock was at a distinct disadvantage. I think the activities of the Committee for an Independent Canada and other like-minded groups helped to draw attention to this sort of thing and I think to some extent were partly successful in getting some of our tax policies and some government policies beamed away from relying totally on that very powerful little clique of investors that have been guiding investment decisions in this country and not making the benefits of those decisions available to ordinary Canadians.
I mentioned the attempts that were successful by Nova Corporation which took advantage of the national energy policy to expand its corporation into a number of areas involving oil and gas. It had very good results, growing in size by three or four times in the course of a mere eight or nine years.
I would also like to bring to the attention of the House some of the options that were experimented with at the same time as those kinds of corporate experiments were going on. There were also experiments by some of the provinces to become involved in attempting to buy back control of their resources and to buy back some industries in control of foreign owners. One of the well-known experiences, at least well-known in my province, is that which Saskatchewan had in taking back control of the potash industry. About 50 per cent of the potash industry came back into Saskatchewan's hands as a result of a Crown corporation being set up with that particular mandate in mind.
What were some of the benefits of gaining that industry and having it held within the province? First, the head office was in the Province of Saskatchewan. It was not in Albuquerque or Chicago, it was in Saskatoon. This meant management decisions were made in Saskatoon. The second and third levels of management tended to be made up of Saskatchewan people and there was a clear decision on the part of the board of directors to attempt to operate that particular industry in a way that would be of benefit to Saskatchewan and create jobs for Saskatchewan residents.
I see, Mr. Speaker, you are signalling that I should come to the end of my remarks. I think these experiments have shown there are other methods of creating investment within the country and that they have clear advantages over relying on foreign investment. I wish the Government would look at some of those before pushing this legislation to the exclusion of these ideas.

Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned before I honestly do not see why this Bill is called Investment Canada. It should be called the Foreign Investment Act. Canadian investors will not receive any benefit from this Bill. It will do nothing for investment in Canada. The benefit will go to the foreign investors. It will certainly not be of benefit to Canadian industry or Canadian employees. I fail to see how the Government can tell us that this Bill will be good for the economy or that it will create jobs and stimulate the economy.
What we are going to become more and more in this country is a branch plant economy. We are going to have more of our industry taken over by American corporations. The tendency will not be for Americans to invest in Canada. They have said they will not invest in Canada. Even following the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in New York they have said that they will not be increasing their investment in Canada at this time and for us not to expect American investors to be waiting at the border, as they call it, with bags of money to invest here.
In light of that, what can we expect? I maintain we can expect very little. In fact, there will be a negative result. For instance, if we have this branch plant economy that I predict, what will the future be for research and development in Canada? Corporations controlled in other countries will not maintain a high level of research and development in Canada in branch plants. They will reduce research and development in Canada. More and more what little research and develop-
Investment Canada Act
ment we have here will filter back to the head offices in the countries of origin of multi-national corporations.
What is the position with respect to exports, Mr. Speaker? If a company has a branch plant in Canada, that branch plant cannot export the product of the parent company. The parent company does the exporting. The branch plant sells the product in the country in which it is located, in this case Canada. What we will have is not only a branch plant but merely a store front where the product of a parent company will be sold in Canada without any avenue or vehicle whatsoever to export that product to other countries. If this Government would put some energy into developing Canadian industry, to fostering research and development to a much larger extent than it has, to fostering and developing Canadian products that we could export, we would be much, much further ahead.
What about the question of parts, machinery and equipment? If these branch plants are part of foreign corporations, then the obligation and the incentive will be to import parts, machinery and equipment from either the subsidiaries of a company in other countries or from the parent company itself.
What will be the situation if we have a downturn in the economy, Mr. Speaker? Which areas will be the first to suffer in the event this transpires? It will be the countries where the branch plants are located. The impetus is to maintain a strong parent company, to maintain the strength of the company in the country of origin where the principal activity is located. It will be the branch plants and the store fronts that will suffer. Here in Canada we will lose our employment and we will be the first to suffer as a result of any further downturns in the economy.
I am not saying all foreign investment is wrong. I do not maintain that in any sense. However, it has to be developed and monitored within a certain framework. The Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) stated that the former Liberal Government was too lenient, that too many foreign companies were allowed to operate in Canada. The Government is saying that we were too strict, that we are rated among our trading partners in the western world as the most inhospitable to foreign investment.
Obviously, with those two polar positions we must have been doing something right. The position that the former Liberal Government took was the correct one and FIRA was the proper way to go. That is not to say FIRA operated perfectly. There were things that had to be modified and should have been modified. Decisions were too slow. There was a dialogue and a consideration that was just not pertinent to what was intended as far as the Canadian economy was concerned.
That is not to say that the vehicle itself did not work. It in fact did work. Even though the Foreign Investment Review Agency did not turn away that many investment prospects in the last few years, the agency was there and everyone knew what it stood for. Before an application was made, it was believed that there had to be some work and some attempt to

January 29, 1985
Investment Canada Act
meet the requirements of FIRA. This was done. By doing that, it provided a very useful service to this country.
Where I see a major problem arising and where the greatest difficulty may be is in the energy sector. At the present time we have very depressed stock prices in certain sectors of the energy industry. If a marketing multi-national or a major company in the marketing field needs a resource base, then we have Canadian companies that are ripe for takeover and purchase. That may be good, it may be not so good. That is not to say that we can disregard that possibility. This Government said it is projecting as a major objective of the Government's energy policy enhanced Canadian participation. If so, how can it reconcile this danger of takeover of Canadian ownership in the energy field? FIRA looked at this and all other possibilities.
The Minister says there will be no Government intervention, no review of takeovers of companies with assets of $5 million of less. I say that there will be no review, period, with this Government. This Government has gone to the United States and said that the door of investment in Canada is open. It said: "Come in, buy our industries, do what you want if you have the money. Just come in and we will look the other way". I fail to see how this Minister, with his attitude for foreign investment and disregard for Canadian ownership, will offer any kind of hindrance or review of the potential but major takeover of Canadian industries. I predict this will be a source of regret by this Government in the not too distant future.
