speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am quite happy to comment both on the motion that has been put forward by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) and also on the idea contained within this Bill. In fact, the proposal which the-
[ Translation]
-by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) in December, to have the subject matter of the Bill referred to a Standing Committee of the House, without referring the Bill itself, is a proposal I accept and support as a Member from the National Capital Region. I could not agree to have the entire Bill with the specific proposals made by the Member for Hull-Aylmer referred to committee.
Since it was quite clear, for instance, from the tone of the comments by the Hon. Member for Gatineau (Mrs. Mailly) that there are some reservations on the other side of the River and also since, in the course of my consultations today, I spoke with the Office of the Mayor of Ottawa and personally with the Mayor of Hull, and they both have serious reservations about this Bill and the way it was proposed, especially since apparently, the Member for Hull-Aylmer did not really consult with the municipal authorities and the two largest municipalities in the region, namely Hull and Ottawa-

In commenting on the proposal of the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier, the principle of referring of the idea that we should find some way of expanding the constitutional recognition of the capital of Canada to include Hull or the Quebec side of the national capital region is something of which I am in favour and at which I am prepared to look. However, I have very severe reservations about the Bill itself and the manner in which it has been put forward by the Hon. Member for Hull-Aylmer (Mr. Isabelle).
I believe the Bill reflects an evolutionary process which has been taking place for most of this century and particularly since the formation of the National Capital Commission some time after the War. De facto but not de jure, the national capital region of the country exists on both the Quebec and the Ontario side. The national capital region is as large or almost as large on the Quebec side as it is on the Ontario side. Substantial numbers of members of the Public Service of Canada and a number of important government departments have now moved to Les Terrasses de la Chaudiere and the other government office buildings which have been built in the last 15 years in the centre of Hull. It is no longer the case that Hull is the poor relation while Ottawa has all of the priority as the capital of Canada. I welcome that.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is a good step forward that over the last 15 years, we have actually started recognizing de facto, the fact that the National Capital is not simply Ottawa, but Ottawa and the Hull area. There is an increasing recognition of the fact that we are a bilingual, a bicultural nation, and this
is why we have a Capital that extends to both our largest provinces and that encompasses two cultures.
I spoke earlier today with the Mayor of Hull, Mr. Michel Legere. He told me about his hope that the City of Hull be seen, in his terms, as a showcase for the Quebec culture, the Francophone reality of our country, a complement to Ottawa, which would presumably be in his view a showcase for the culture, for the Anglophone and perhaps the multicultural reality of this country.

I certainly accept that, Mr. Speaker, but I have reservations. I support the idea of referring only the subject matter of the Bill because of the manner in which the Hon. Member for Hull-Aylmer put forward this particular Bill.
This Bill provoked a great deal of concern when it was debated in the House of Commons in December. I share those concerns because the intentions of the Hon. Member for Hull-Aylmer are in fact greater than those of the Bill itself. The Hon. Member for Hull-Aylmer made no bones about his view that this Bill should be the first step toward the formation of a federal district for the national capital of Canada which would apparently be comparable to the federal district of Washington, the District of Columbia, in the United States. He said this quite explicitly. This was not a hidden agenda but an agenda that was very direct and overt. In debate on December 7, at page 1028 of Hansard, he said:
-it would be a first step towards the establishment of what many people wish to see, a federal district.
On page 1029, he went on to say:
Moreover, if we consider what some politicians have said during the years, the best way to administer the national capital region would be to establish a federal district.
Later on in debate he said:
-the Government must have the necessary tools in the decision-making process.
In other words, he was discussing a federal district which, I suppose, would be along the lines of that proposed by Mr. Douglas Fullerton in his report on the national capital of 1973 or 1974. In that particular report, Mr. Fullerton proposed that there should be some form of amalgamation of municipalities and that there should be a supra-national or supra-governmen-tal authority that would take in the municipal officials, perhaps the provincial officials and the federal Government. That would provide government for close to a million people who are living in the national capital region. I do not know who all these people are.
Frankly, I do not know those people who so enthusiastically seek and promote the establishment of a federal district similar to Washington's Federal District in the United States. I do not know them. I have been a politician in this area for close to fifteen years yet, during all that time I do not think I have ever met one citizen in this area who supported the idea of a federal
January 29, 1985

district, with the possible exception of Mr. Fullerton who is one of my constituents in Ottawa Centre.

On the other hand, I have heard a great deal against such a position. The negative opinions against a federal district have been voiced whenever the issue has surfaced. For example, that negative opinion surfaced in response to the proposal which Mr. Fullerton brought forward in the early 1970s. There was a parliamentary committee established to study the Fullerton report. The municipalities of the region either boycotted the committee or when representatives came forward they were not prepared to say anything constructive because they felt- and I think correctly-that it was wrong to deprive the people of this region of access to the kinds of government which they had had for decades upon decades, both the municipal and provincial authorities.
Many of my constituents in Ottawa Centre work in high-tech industries. Others work at Loblaws or the Bay. Others are trying to organize because they work at Eaton's. Some of them are consultants or people who have brought a business to Ontario because they like the ambiance of Ottawa. Those people may have nothing at all to do with the federal Government, except that they happen to live in the city where the federal Government has its headquarters. Many people who work for the federal Government share the views of those who have nothing to do with the federal Government. They do not want to incur the risks of losing provincial medicare, the system of law and the priorities which they have had for a long time through the creation of a federal district. They fear a form of government-a national capital commission or a group of commissioners appointed by the Cabinet or the Prime Minister-which would sit on a co-equal basis with the Mayor of Ottawa and the Mayor of Hull. Possibly there would not be a Mayor of Ottawa or a Mayor of Hull.
The people I have talked with about this issue over the course of many years have grave reservations about that kind of venture. They see it as something which is unknown. I believe they would also resent some of the comments which were made by the Hon. Member for Hull-Aylmer (Mr. Isabelle) in his contribution to the debate. For example, he indicated that he was very disturbed by the municipal planning which had taken place. In his view it had the effect of blocking out the House of Commons. He said:
Beauty is not the only issue but Parliament must be "at home", as they say, except that in this case the Ottawa municipality has control over it, which is a nonsense, if I may say so.
I think the Hon. Member ignored the fact that in the planning of the City of Ottawa, which came after the Greber report, and when the downtown area was planned in the early 1960s, specific regard was had in trying to recognize the pre-eminence of the Peace Tower and the House Commons. We, in our wisdom today, may judge that wrong, but nonetheless anyone who examines downtown Ottawa will discover that the height limits have the effect of creating a saucer, so that the House of Commons and the Peace Tower remain the pre-eminent buildings in this part of the downtown core. The
Constitution Act, 1867
buildings are only allowed to get higher as they get farther away from Wellington Street and the parliamentary precinct. Today that may be seen as naive planning, but it was clearly designed to take account of the fact that Parliament Hill is an important national symbol and should be given that pre-eminence.
The planning of the City of Ottawa in those days-and I was a member of the municipal council for part of that time- was carried out in close conjunction with the National Capital Commission. That remains the case to this day. I could cite the example of the location of the new courthouse which is being built in my riding at the corner of Laurier Avenue and Elgin Street. In that particular case the National Capital Commission played a very strong role. When the city said that the building should be oriented toward Elgin Street, the National Capital Commission, acting on behalf of the citizens of Canada, said no. The National Capital Commission felt that it was an important building and a symbol of the presence of the Province of Ontario in the national capital. They decreed that the building should be oriented toward the canal and the National Arts Centre rather than toward Elgin Street. The NCC won. So it is hardly the case that the control of the City of Ottawa is making a nonsense of the respect for this community, which is also the national capital.
What I am concerned about is that if one pursues the concept of the Bill, one must be aware of the kind of sensitivities which were reflected in the debate in December. [Translation]
I have in mind for instance the comments made by the Hon. Member for Gatineau (Mrs. Mailly). She said that the population of the City of Gatineau exceeds by 20,000 that of the City of Hull. Even if Hull is the core of the urban population on the Quebec side of the National Capital area, there is now a sort of competition between Gatineau and Hull and this must be recognized.
Frankly, I do not know how to react to that. Are we to establish a national capital to be called Ottawa-Hull-Gatineau or, since Nepean's population is almost similar to that of Gatineau, should it be Ottawa-Hull-Gatineau-Nepean, or are Gloucester or Cumberland going to have their day? I do not know.
Clearly there are problems and they can be studied if the matter is referred to a committee of this House. However, a referral of the Bill as such would do two things in my view, Mr. Speaker. On the one hand, it could give rise to reactions from certain people from both sides of the river who would suggest for instance, as we say in English:

"The capital of Canada was always meant to be Ottawa". They are rednecks who have not understood that this country has changed since Confederation. Perhaps at that time the Fathers of Confederation did not understand that our country should be joined together; two equal and kindly peoples who should come together. They were not prepared to recognize

January 29, 1985
Constitution Act, 1867
that. There is no question that in the capital of Canada les Quebecois et les Hullois were junior partners for a long time. That has now changed.
To name Hull in a Bill and to send the Bill forward and attempt to bring it back to the House for third reading without having considered some of the alternatives seems to me a bit short-sighted. It would be very provocative as well if we were to send a Bill forward with the connotations which have been given it by the Hon. Member for Hull-Aylmer, and specifically his suggestion that this was the first step in the creation of a federal district. I would be extremely uneasy about that, and so would my constituents. I would also suggest that the constituents of the Hon. Member would be uneasy. I would place on the record the fact that in the election of 1980 the Hon. Member for Hull-Aylmer had a majority of 17,500, but his majority shrank to some 1,500 or 1,600 in the 1984 election. Perhaps that suggests that he does not have that many constituents who are keen on this particular suggestion, which he has put forward on numerous occasions, particularly in view of the lack of adequate consultation with a number of people-municipal leaders and others-who deserve to be consulted on this subject.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION ACT, 1867 AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE HULL IN NATIONAL CAPITAL REGION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member for Ottawa West, I am pleased to rise to address both the motion and the Bill. I, in fact, am the only Hon. Member on this side of the House whose constituency is entirely within the boundaries of the City of Ottawa. I am therefore particularly pleased to participate in a debate which has become something of a tradition in this House, the debate initiated by the Hon. Member for Hull-Aylmer (Mr. Isabelle), perhaps not every year but most years, on the subject of Canada's national capital. The Hon. Member has been introducing such a Bill on a regular basis since 1967, and if there have been years when he has not introduced such a Bill, he has compensated for that lack by offering it twice, as he did in 1984. In fact, one year ago this month, during the second session of the Thirty-Second Parliament, a not dissimilar Bill was introduced by the Hon. Member and it is a tribute to his consistency and resilience that he persists with his proposal.
The theme is always the same, Mr. Speaker, but contains, however, its variations. On this occasion we do not have a proposal to change the name of the capital of Canada from Ottawa to "the national capital region" or to some such anonymous equivalent but, as I understand it, it is proposed to call it "Ottawa-Hull" instead of "Ottawa".
This theme of renaming or reorganizing the national capital of Canada did not, of course, originate with the Hon. Member for Hull-Aylmer, although after 17 years I think he might be forgiven for thinking that he has acquired squatters' rights on the territory. The argument for creation of a federal district to serve the national capital has recurred on a regular basis for many years. One local observer wrote in 1962 that it was only a matter of time before such a district was created. He was quite sure, in fact, that it would be established before the centennial celebrations of 1967. That deadline having expired at the time the Hon. Member for Hull-Aylmer began his own introduction of motions and Bills on this matter in this House-perhaps as his own centennial project-the question now is whether such a district will be created before the centennial anniversary of the Hon. Member's efforts.
The arguments on this subject predate all of this, however. They go back to Confederation itself. Ottawa was not, contrary to a popular and inaccurate impression, chosen on a whim of Queen Victoria as the capital of Canada. Careful study was made of competing sites, such as Kingston, Toronto, Quebec City, Montreal and Ottawa, before a decision was made. Ottawa was chosen because it offered many advantages which it continues to offer today. Its people and its culture were a hybrid of our two founding peoples. It was located on the border of Upper Canada and Lower Canada. It had, and
January 29, 1985

still has, of course, great natural beauty. Those Hon. Members who will be participating in tonight's parliamentary hockey game in connection with the Winterlude celebrations will attest to the fact that it has an exhilarating and bracing winter climate, which we all enjoy!
The debate on the location of Canada's capital was heated and continued for many years prior to Confederation. Debate has continued since, not, I am happy to say, on the location but on the administrative organization of our capital. The Bill of the Hon. Member for Hull-Aylmer is a continuation of a debate which is as old as our country. In 1872 one of the fathers of Confederation, John Hamilton Gray, had this to say on the issue:
At the time of the convention, one mistake occurred: no provision was made for creating a federal district for the capital and withdrawing it from the exclusive control of the local legislature of any one of the provinces.
That which was designed to be the capital of the Confederation might fairly rest its claim for support upon the people of the Dominion. Its order, well-being, sanitary arrangements, police regulations, adornments and improvements are essential to the comfort and security not only of the representatives who attend Parliament, but of all those who are compelled to resort to it as the capital of the country in the discharge of the various duties attendant upon the administration of public affairs.
In language reminiscent of that of the Hon. Member for Hull-Aylmer Mr. Gray went on to say:
Its reputation should be national, not provincial. It belongs no more to Ontario than it does to New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Quebec or any of the provinces constituting the confederation.
He then went on to say, and it is something with which the residents of Ottawa would probably agree.
The expenses incident to its civic control must necessarily be far greater than would evolve upon it if merely an ordinary municipality. It is no answer to say that increased value and property is sufficient consideration for the increased burden put upon its inhabitants.
Since then the debate has continued, Mr. Speaker, always with the same basic arguments; first, that the national capital should not be part of any one province and, second, that the capital itself would be better administered by eliminating the jurisdictional overlap which now exists between varying federal, provincial and municipal authorities in the national capital region.
The Hon. Member has not suggested, at least not in this particular Bill, that a federal district should be created. He just suggests that Hull be included in the national capital. However, I think I agree with my friend, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), that it is obvious that the creation of a federal district is what the Hon. Member for Hull-Aylmer has in mind. He has certainly supported this idea in the past. Last year, in fact, during a debate on a Bill in the last Parliament, he discussed the difficulties of administration in the national capital region, concluding, and I quote:
This is why over the years I have always advocated a federal district, in order that the federal Government be at home here.
Frankly, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that after 117 years the federal Government has made itself quite at home in Ottawa. The arguments in favour of the creation of a federal district, particularly the administrative arguments, do have some merit and perhaps we should be studying such a pro-
Constitution Act, 1867
posal. But we have to ask ourselves-and I am sure the people of Canada would ask us this question-whether the creation of such a district would be worth the trouble it would take to do so. If we think we have jurisdictional problems now, they would be nothing compared to the problems we would have in trying to persuade the Governments of Ontario and Quebec to cede territory to a new federal district.
Is this, after all, the most important issue on the national agenda? Are constitutional questions at all of prime importance to the Canadian people at this point in time, particularly after years of acrimonious constitutional debate and at a time when questions of national and international economic problems, issues of famine and world peace might reasonably be expected to be on the minds of parliamentarians? And of all the possible constitutional questions which might be discussed, is the creation of a new administrative entity for the national capital something which should take priority? Should it take priority, for example, over the question of Quebec's participation in a constitutional accord? Should it take precedence over creation of new administrative arrangements for the people of the north who have been living, really, under a quasi-colonial administration for years? Is the question of administrative reorganization of the capital more important than resolving important constitutional issues and questions of human rights concerning the native peoples of this country?
I do not think we would find much support throughout this country if we were to devote much of our time to this issue right now. It would take time, Mr. Speaker. The Hon. Member for Hull-Aylmer and other Members of this House were involved some years ago in committee deliberations on this issue, deliberations which took months of work and the energy of many people. It is a complex issue which cannot be resolved by a quick debate in this House, not if we wish to do justice to it. It would again take deliberation and some delicate constitutional negotiations. The fact is, and I say this as someone who is not without sympathy for the efforts of the Hon. Member, and as someone who, having lived in Ottawa almost half of his life, is familiar with the problems of living here, that I think we are reasonably well off in this area.
The situation is not perfect; there are administrative overlaps. Jurisdictional issues can be confusing, as anyone who has dealt with three or four different police forces in a day can attest to. But things work. Life goes on. We manage to make this city, this whole region, work, and it works well enough to be considered a desirable residential area for many people. It could be improved and a federal district, properly structured, could be a positive change. But the return on our investment of energy and time would be insufficient to justify undertaking such a reform at this time.
How would the different legal systems of Quebec and Ontario be reconciled in one new territory? I assume that the Hon. Member would want Hull to be included in such a territory. What about local self-government, Mr. Speaker? We would not want to turn the capital into another domestic

January 29, 1985
Constitution Act, 1867
colony, disenfranchising the people of this area who, whatever the complications, at least now have many opportunities to vote for various elected bodies. We would not want to restrict the political activities of people residing here. A large proportion of our local population has already suffered that infringement on their political rights-public servants who are denied the right to speak out on important issues concerning their lives.
What political system would a new national capital have, Mr. Speaker? Would territorial councils be created to do the essential work now done by municipal councils on both sides of the river? Would there be one territorial council for the whole area or two? If there were only one, and it seems logical to have only one, if one of the arguments in favour of creating a federal district is to reduce jurisdictional confusion, then what protection would there be for the minority residing on the Quebec side of the Ottawa River?
How would federal and local interests be resolved under a new political system, Mr. Speaker? Presumably voters in the district would not be disenfranchised federally any more than they would at the municipal level and would continue to elect Members of Parliament. It is clear that a territorial legislature would not have the same independence as a province, because the whole raison d'etre of this proposal is to remove the capital from a province and facilitate treatment of what are viewed as national concerns in the administration of the capital. Would federal representatives be appointed to a territorial council, and what balance would there be between elected and appointed officials?
The questions go on and on, Mr. Speaker, and resolving them would take years of negotiation beforehand, and years of conflict, compromise and adjustment during implementation. The fact is that no matter how simple a policy or plan may seem to be, it is never simple in implementation. This is one plan which would be complicated in its development, and undoubtedly acrimonious and unpredictable in implementation. In a perfect world, a federal district serving as the capital might be worth while; but in the real world, the world we live in, we look for the best workable solution. In an imperfect world, we establish priorities, weigh our resources, and apply them to the urgent problems before we deal with what is merely desirable. This type of administrative and political reform for the capital might be desirable, but it is certainly not urgent.
The Hon. Member might then say well, why not just proceed with his Bill today, as an interim measure, to amend the Constitution, and include Hull as part of the national capital? The Hon. Member's Bill would go further than that. It would permit Parliament also to prescribe in the Constitution other surrounding areas as part of the capital of Canada. And in fact, if the name of the capital is going to be changed to Ottawa-Hull, why not, after all, include Nepean, Gloucester, Vanier, Aylmer or Gatineau? What is the magic barrier, the invisible demarcation line which would prevent other areas from also being so included? The fact is, Mr. Speaker, the capital does draw its character from the people beyond the
bounds of the City of Ottawa. Thousands of people who work for the Government of Canada reside in areas outside the City of Ottawa and, as the Hon. Member has noted in the past, many of the people who do reside in Ottawa work in government buildings in his constituency as they do in mine.
No one denies that there is interaction and that the interaction between Ottawa and the surrounding areas of the national capital region is important to the culture and character of the city. The interactions which form our characters as individuals, as groups, as cities, have virtually no limit. Today the capital of Canada is Ottawa. Tomorrow the capital would be Ottawa-Hull if the Hon. Member's wishes were realized. The day after, who knows? We might speak of the capital as Ottawa-Hull-Nepean-Gloucester- Vanier-Aylmer-Gatineau.
The next move would be to return to the Hon. Member's earlier suggestion to rename the area "the national capital area", or something similar. Such a name would be easier on the ears than a hyphenated melange, but oh so gray, so soulless, so boring!
It would always be possible to substitute an Indian name for this bleak administrative title; Algonquin, perhaps? Asticou? How about that variation on the old Indian word, Ottawa? It has a certain ring to it, it has all of the historical connections, the roots and tradition of this country, that a national capital should have. It is not an imported name; it is a proud local name, recognized throughout this country and throughout the world as the home of our Parliament and the capital of Canada.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION ACT, 1867 AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE HULL IN NATIONAL CAPITAL REGION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise this afternoon on behalf of the constituents of Nepean-Carleton to share their concern over the Bill before us and the amendment related thereto. I want to preface my remarks this afternoon by complimenting the two previous speakers and conveying to the House the fact that I endorse the concerns they presented to us in the course of this afternoon's debate.
National capitals around the world are governed in different ways. Many systems are in place in Washington, Canberra, Moscow, London and others. There are advantages and disadvantages to the different types of government which exist in the various nations around the world. However, the bottom line is that no perfect system has yet been identified for national capitals.
The Bill before us obviously has merit in many respects, but the thing that raised my real concern was when the sponsor of the Bill indicated that this was really a first step towards the creation of a national capital district. It is that aspect of it, Mr. Speaker, that concerns me more fundamentally than any other aspect. I agree with the Member for Ottawa West (Mr. Daubney), relative to the earlier studies into the creation of a national capital district for the capital of Canada, that there is no local support for this type of approach to national government. We have had this debate many times but most recently in the early 1970s when this community had a dramatic and heart-rending debate on the particular issue. The consensus that came out of that was that there was no heart, no desire,
January 29, 1985

no will and few advantages to be gained by that type of a national government system for the nation's capital.
Ottawa, the nation's capital, is situated at the confluence of the Ottawa and Rideau Rivers. It is a sight that has tremendous natural beauty. The area is underlain by pre-Cambrian rocks which are a billion or more years old. Sitting on top of the pre-Cambrian terrain which extends for many hundreds of kilometers is a thin veneer of Ordovician rock, roughly 580 million years old. Those pre-Cambrian and Ordovician rocks are the basis of the local physiography of the area.
As the millenniums moved on this area was covered by a thick ice sheet 20,000, 30,000 and 40,000 years ago. We are unable to tell how thick this ice sheet was locally, but it was sufficiently thick and sufficiently heavy to cause the local area to be depressed as much as 180 to 260 feet. As this ice melted the rebound associated with it was very low and the area was inundated, 16,000 to 20,000 years ago, by what we now refer to as the Champlain Sea.
The invasion of the Champlain Sea was a god's blessing, if one can put it that way. The sediments that were deposited out of that sea, known as the Champlain sediments, have provided us, in the St. Lawrence and Ottawa River valleys, with the tremendously good agricultural lands which exist locally. If it was not for that invasion of the sea not so many years ago, this would be a barren pre-Cambrian terrain with no capability of food production.
Once the rebound was complete and the Champlain Sea withdrew 12,000 to 16,000 years ago, a tremendous forest developed locally. It was one of the prime pine timber forests that the world was ever to see. It was in that environment that the Algonquin and Iroquois families and communities developed and grew and fought with one another and others. In the course of time, in the early 1600s, Champlain moved through this terrain briefly, I believe in 1600 and 1602. The next white person to move through the community was Nicholas Gatineau Duplessis. He came down what is now the Gatineau River and named the area of that great valley.
Many, many years were to go by before there was much inluence on the Algonquin and Iroquois communities. It was not until 1798 and 1799 when a man by the name of Philemon Wright, who was then living in Woburn, Massachusetts, came on two exploration expeditions into what is now called the Ottawa valley. He was a farmer, a cattleman, a puritan in faith I am told, and Kentish in extraction. In the winter of 1800 and 1801 he moved with his family and five other families from Massachusetts into the Ottawa Valley and settled in what is now the City of Hull. He was the first of the timber barons and farmers to settle locally.
Perhaps the next highlight of our local history was the arrival of Colonel John By in 1827. He arrived on behalf of the Government of England to build the canal between Kingston and Ottawa. On his arrival the village on the south side of the river became known as Bytown, named after Colonel John By. In 1847 Bytown was incorporated as a town with a mayor and
Constitution Act, 1867
a council. Its first mayor was a man named John Scott. In the course of time he became a federal Member of Parliament for this particular area. It was not until 1854 that the name was changed from Bytown to Ottawa through an Act passed by the Legislative Assembly of United Canada. In this period Ottawa was chosen by Queen Victoria to become the seat of government for the new country of Canada.
In 1860 the Prince of Wales, then 17 years of age and perhaps better known as the Duke of Newcastle, visited Canada. During the course of his visit in 1860 he laid the cornerstone for the Parliament building of Canada. That is something we should be aware of. From that date forward what we now know as the parliamentary precinct in Ottawa has grown.
In the years that followed the National Capital Commission and the national capital district was formed. In 1969 we had superimposed on our local area a form of regional government which was created by the Province of Ontario. The Ottawa-Carleton regional Government was the first such system of regional government to be developed anywhere in Canada.
In the greater Ottawa community we have three tiers of government at the moment. We have that tier which relates to the activities of the National Capital Commission, we have that tier which relates to the regional municipality of Ottawa-Carleton and we have that tier which relates to the local municipalities such as the City of Nepean, the City of Ottawa or the Township of Rideau.
The National Capital Commission is responsible for many activities in the national capital district. We must make this distinction clear. It is responsible for certain aspects of planning. It is responsible for the development of parks, for certain national driveways, and for certain educational activities on the south side of the Ottawa River. It has other responsibilities which are partly different in the Province of Quebec. It is responsible, of course, for the well-being, planning and management of the parliamentary precinct in addition to the things I have just mentioned.
For a short but precious period in my life I had the privilege of being a councillor in the regional government to which all of the local municipalities belong. That regional level of government is responsible for all health care locally. It is responsible for sewer and water and for the upper level of planning. It is responsible for the regional road system, for public transit and for everything associated with the local welfare system. It is a reasonably democratic system of government. It is locally, awkwardly expensive. However, I believe the quality associated with what the region does is beneficial for the greater Ottawa community.
That has been its track record and involvement. Its activities are very long lasting. Many of us do not realize this locally, but we have incorporated in our sewer and water system in the regional municipality some of the most advanced technologies that exist anywhere in North America.

January 29, 1985
Constitution Act, 1867
While some of us may debate this issue in the winter months, we have a splendid public transit system. Few of us realize that currently over 70 per cent of the work trips into the core of the Ottawa area are made by public transit. The goal of our local public transit is to have 80 per cent of the work trips into the core area by public transit. I am sure that with the creation of the new bus ways and related features, that goal will be accomplished.
The municipal system of government, such as those in the Cities of Ottawa, Nepean, Gloucester and Vanier and in the Townships of Osgoode, Rideau, Goulburn and the City of Kanata, was set up originally in 1851 and 1852 and amended at various times in the interim period. However, it involves the election of a mayor or reeve and a council to their respective corporations.
Within that local system of government to which people are now elected for three-year terms, one of the tremendous advantages is the ability of the ordinary citizen to interface with that level of government. It is possible to call one's local councillor this afternoon and tomorrow evening at the council meeting the matter can be resolved. Matters move very quickly. Many of the activities related to this lower tier of government is related to voluntarism. This is something that is very precious.
For instance, in the south end of my riding the fire protection service is provided by volunteer fire departments. They are people who are willing to give freely of their time at any hour of the day or night to respond to a local emergency. All of the recreation activities in those communities are provided on a volunteer basis. The library system is run on a volunteer basis. Most of the recreation is supervised and organized on a volunteer basis.
At the same time I think it is also fair to say that most of the planning is developed locally and on a volunteer basis. Therefore, it is a splendid system of government that we have, with volunteers and elected councillors working together in a community for the over-all benefit of its citizens.
Quite apart from this type of regional and municipal government that those of us who live locally find so valuable and precious is a tremendous educational system. In this instance it is associated with the Province of Ontario but that is not terribly important. Most of the local educational system has been developed by local input in which we have daycare centres, French immersion programs in primary and elementary schools and public and separate school systems. The community is integrated into one of the best educational systems which I believe exists anywhere in Canada. Perhaps few places around the world would excel in comparison to it.
The citizens of the greater Ottawa community have developed this tremendous system of local education with local input, pride and opportunities. In this milieu over the years we have had the creation and development of two great universities, the University of Ottawa and Carleton University, as well as Algonquin College. If we should proceed in the direction anticipated by this Bill, would these universities lose their local identity? Would they, by necessity, have to become the national universities of Canada? What would their relation be to the Province of Ontario? What would their relation be to their local community? How would they be governed and financed? As national universities, would their responsibilities be to the local community or to citizens from St. John's to Vancouver? One wonders about that.
As a local Member of Parliament and a person who has been involved in this community for approximately 25 years, there are many concerns associated with the potential creation of a national capital district and the government that would be associated with that. If we had a national district created here, one could imagine that the form of government which would be superimposed upon it would probably be identical to that in which the National Capital Commission is presently governed. There would be a chairperson who, while chosen because of their qualities, would probably also be chosen for political reasons. There would be councillors chosen for political reasons. According to the present constitution of the National Capital Commission, I believe only three or four of that group are from the local area.
In that system there is no way of influencing these people. They are not accountable to the local population in any way. They do not need to listen because they have no reason to. They have another master. There is nothing in the system that makes them accountable and keeps them attuned to the local needs. Naturally, as Canadians they would have pride in the national capital, but beyond that their interests would be much different from the ongoing interests of those of us who have the privilege of living in the lower regions of the Rideau valley and along the south shore of the Ottawa River.
While I am sure the intent of an alliance between Hull and Ottawa as part of a nation's capital is well intended and those of us who have come to learn the value and traditions of the two cultures locally could think of nothing but having the opportunity of strengthening those relationships, the animal that this Bill might lead us to is not the way that the residents of Nepean-Carleton want to go. Nor do I believe it is the direction in which the residents of Ottawa-Carleton want to go. I would urge Members of the House not to proceed with this Bill for the reasons I have given.

subtopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-ACTIVITIES OF CHEQUE CASHING COMPANIES. (B) REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION
CONSUMER AFFAIRS-ACTIVITIES OF CHEQUE CASHING COMPANIES. (B) REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I put two questions to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) arising out of a report in my own City of Winnipeg that one of the cheque cashing companies-not a small company, one with 20 branches across the country-on Christmas Eve charged a mother who was on welfare $76 to cash a cheque for $466. The cheque was dated December 28. The company charged this woman $76 to cash her cheque four days early that is, on December 24. The interest rate was 21 per cent. When one talks about interest rates, one talks about interest rates for a year. The annual rate, therefore, would have been 21 per cent. This company cashed the cheque on December 24 and was able to get the face value of the cheque, namely $466, four days later. That 21 per cent interest was in fact calculated on an annual basis, more than 2,500 per cent.
It is not Members of Parliament, doctors, lawyers, businessmen, or even skilled workers who have to go to one of these cheque cashing companies to get money a few days before the cheque is legally cashable, it is poor people, native people, and people on welfare. These companies are ripping off people who are in most desperate situations. These companies are victimizing people. What they are doing may be legal, and I shall come to that in a moment, but it is certainly highly immoral.
In the office of this money cashing organization is a sign which reads that it charges from 10 per cent to 21 per cent to cash post-dated cheques. There is a provision in the Small Loans Act which reads:
"criminal rate" means an effective annual rate of interest calculated in accordance with generally accepted actuarial practices and principles that exceeds sixty per cent-
That is 60 per cent a year, I presume.
I asked the Minister to investigate what happened. This was not an isolated case. If we believe this company to which I refer was breaking the law it should be prosecuted. If the company is not breaking the law, then there is something wrong with the law.
What we want the Department to do after investigation is to come back and bring legislation to the House. If legislation is not needed, it should tell the House what will be done to stop this kind of completely unacceptable rip-off. This is not the first time this matter has been brought to the attention of the Government. The National Anti-Poverty Organization brought the matter to the attention of the former Liberal
Adjournment Debate
Government. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) brought this to the attention of the then Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs last March, almost a year ago. At that time the then Minister said:
Unfortunately it is too late to do much this year, but I can assure the Hon. Member that a new system will be in place by the next taxation year.
The new system obviously is not in place. The present Minister said:
I would like to reassure the Hon. Member and say that we are closely monitoring the situation. There is no law forbidding such uses and we shall bring in appropriate solutions in due time.
I want the Minister and the Department to bring in those appropriate solutions now, or in a very short period of time, not at some time in the future. I urge the Minister to take action quickly on behalf of the poorest people who have to go to this kind of company.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-ACTIVITIES OF CHEQUE CASHING COMPANIES. (B) REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 28, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) asked two questions, the first regarding cheque cashing services offered by certain businesses, and the second regarding tax rebate discounting services. With respect to the Hon. Member's question on cheque cashing operations, I wish to advise the House that this matter is under consideration.
The Hon. Member has suggested that we investigate these businesses. He has raised this matter before, and I appreciate it being brought to the attention of the Ministry and this House. As he indicated, these companies been established quickly over the past few years. Then cash various types of cheques for a fee. I understand that the fees range from 2 to 10 per cent for most cheques, although they may range from 12 to 21 per cent for post-dated cheques. This fee takes into account that services are provided during non banking hours, usually from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., six days per week and sometimes on Sundays.
On reviewing the Act, it is not clear that the fee for these services can be interpreted as a rate of interest. If this were the case, it would be up to the Attorney General of each province to prosecute, if indeed there was a rate of interest charged that exceeded the maximum rate permitted under the Criminal Code. Currently under review is the rate of 12 to 21 per cent and whether it is a charge or a rate of interest. These businesses offer a service for which many Canadians are prepared to pay. Their reason for doing so may derive from such legitimate interests as greater convenience. As stated previously, the Department is aware of the Hon. Member's concerns and we appreciate him bringing them to our attention.
With respect to tax rebate discounting services, the Hon. Member can be assured that discounting transactions are monitored to ensure that they comply with the federal legislation. Indeed, there have been prosecutions under the Tax Rebate Discounting Act.
I wish to remind the House of the purpose of this Act. It is to protect the interests of taxpayers who give up the right to their anticipated tax refund in exchange for a minimun of 85

subtopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD-REQUEST FOR EARLY PAY-OUT TO FARMERS
CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD-REQUEST FOR EARLY PAY-OUT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this question is further to my question yesterday which was erroneously listed under the heading of the Canadian Wheat Board, while it in fact related to the Western Grain Stabilization Act.
The difficulties in western agriculture are obvious, 1 believe. There is a very serious cash flow problem resulting from two factors, the first being the cost-price squeeze and the second being the credit squeeze. The cost-price aspect of it is evident. On the income side, the price of grain has dropped over the past few years and producers were making it on volume; they produced more and more grain. The 1984 drought and the consequent short crop has exacerbated the problem. On the expense side, fertilizer, chemicals, equipment and fuel costs and the cost of money or interest rates all continue to add to the farmers' burden.
In response to this, last July at Prince Albert the Progressive Conservative Party announced a number of commitments to western Canada, undertakings that were designed to emphasize the inclusion of western Canada as a partner in Confederation. After 20 years of exclusion, we in western Canada feel that we are now doing quite well.
Already a number of promises have been horoured. We are represented by some 13 Cabinet Ministers. We have reduced the price of fuel to producers, including western farmers, by some 28 cents a gallon. Interest rates have gone down some 2.5 points since election day. Some rail lines that were destined for abandonment have been restored and revitalized. Farm Credit Corporation loan interest rates have been reduced for a certain category of borrower.
I also recall that at Prince Albert, we indicated that we would amend legislation to permit quicker government reaction time on such legislation as the Western Grain Stabilization Act in order that it be more responsive to economic trends and to the immediate needs of the producers. There are clearly a number of reasons why this Government should follow through with its commitment to amend the Western Grain Stabilization Act to allow for an interim payment this spring. I would like to elaborate on these reasons and to ask the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) to reply.
The overwhelming reason why an interim payment is needed stems from the drought which ravaged the prairies last
summer. At least five million tonnes of grain were lost. With a potential value of $200 per tonne, that represents a direct loss of about $1 billion to Canadian farmers, and indirectly to all of the companies which provide input and services for them. In addition to the losses due to drought, many farmers in northeastern Saskatchewan and in central Manitoba suffered grain losses due to excessive moisture. These losses come on the heels of the losses of previous years.
Last year, western farmers spent some $1.4 billion on direct crop inputs including seed, fertilizer, pesticides and other supplies. Most of this was required in the spring. This year the costs will be even higher. Statistics Canada indicates a projected increase of about 5 per cent. What is more, the price of grain which was poor last year is expected to drop slightly in the coming year.
A considerable amount of publicity was generated by the announcement in December that Canadian farmers' realized net income rose by 14 per cent in 1984. That figure is quite misleading in view of the fact that realized net income, the cash that farmers actually receive, does not take into account inventory changes. The gain which amounted to 15 per cent on the prairies was only achieved through a very considerable reduction in inventory. Farmers delivered most of the grain they had in storage.
If one looks at real net income from last year's crop, one sees that it is down by over 50 per cent on the prairies. Saskatchewan's real net income was down by some $400 million, Alberta's by some $220 million and Manitoba, rebounding from an impossibly bad previous year, had a gain of only $140 million.
It would be foolish to suppose that the money paid out by the federal Government for crop insurance, stabilization, final Wheat Board payments and drought assistance will carry farmers through the planting season. In a great many cases, the money has already gone to creditors for last year's crop.
It is true that most of the young and beginning farmers are the ones who are most deeply in debt. These are also the people on whom we will need to count to produce our future food supplies. These young farmers have a heavy debt load as a result of land purchases which were made at high prices. Over the last couple of years, through rising expenses and falling grain prices, there has been a turnaround in land prices. Land prices have fallen dramatically and the lending institutions-the banks and the credit unions-have moved their attention away from asset values as a basis for lending, and now, quite properly, look at cashflow. I say, "quite properly" because without cashflow there cannot be repayment. One wishes that as much attention had been paid by borrower and lender alike to cashflow when land prices were rising as is being paid to them as the prices fall.
Many institutions which loaned money on the strength of fair market value of assets see their security eroding and consequently are calling in their loans. Many are now refusing operating credit to those producers who are in bad shape.
January 29, 1985

Those caught in this credit squeeze will have trouble borrowing operating funds for spring seeding. There is now a very urgent need for an interim payment under the Western Grain Stabilization Plan. I do not mean the kind of payment that the Liberals made. That was a cynical offering made in August, two weeks before the federal election. That was the kind of manipulation which we in the West came to expect and know so well. 1 am talking about a sincere and timely response to a western problem; the kind of response which was contemplated when the Prince Albert declaration was formulated. The Government should be looking at making an interim payment to help farmers meet the heavy financial commitment of spring seeding. 1 would ask the Minister to move swiftly to present amending legislation which would permit an interim payment in time for spring seeding.
Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of State (Canadian Wheat
Board)): Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member opposite for giving me a chance to respond to his concerns. I assure him that the Government shares many of the concerns he has expressed. We have taken some steps, not only on behalf of western farmers, but on behalf of all farmers in Canada.
In the statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on November 8, we significantly reduced the tax on farm fuels. Admittedly, there is still a considerable amount of tax on farm fuels, but the federal Government recognizes that there is a problem and it is taking steps to improve that. Last week the Government introduced legislation to amend the Agricultural Stabilization Act. That will allow for a voluntary tripartite red meat stabilization program in Canada. Just before Christmas we announced for the first time the invoking of the meat import quotas under the provisions of a Bill which was passed by the previous Government.
I would like to mention another item which will benefit western farmers. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankow-ski) has frozen the seaway tolls, in response to the concerns of farmers over rising costs.
Let me directly address the question of the Hon. Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Wilson). We certainly anticipate being able to make an interim payment. We have legislation which will be introduced very shortly. As I said yesterday in response to his question, I very much appreciate the co-operation-as I am sure do western farmers-which has been indicated from both opposition parties in assuring us that they will pass the legislation very quickly.
The larger question is: What do we do with the Western Grain Stabilization Act? It has been roughly ten years since that legislation was implemented and I think that is a sufficient period of time to know how the Act works. There is good evidence that the Act should be reviewed. The Government will look at it as quickly as possible.
I have heard representations that the Government should take into account more individual records of producers, so that there will not have to be a major crop failure on the Prairies in order to trigger a payout. I have also heard concerns that there
Adjournment Debate
should be provisions in the Act which would allow people who grow and feed their own grain to contribute to the plan.
The Government will be acting very quickly to allow for an interim payment in time for the spring seeding. We fully recognize the cash shortage problem facing prairie farmers, and we also very much appreciate the contribution that they make to the national economy.
We will also be looking as quickly as we can at what can be done, and I have already had some input from some provincial Governments. We welcome input from other people on what we should do with the Act on a longer term basis to make it more responsive so we do not have to ask for legislation to make an interim payment. The Act will be there. It will be responsive, and we will not have to make amendments in order to make payments to producers who are in need of cash.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING-CHARTERED BANKS' REFUSAL TO CASH WELFARE CHEQUES. (B) EXISTENCE OF CHEQUE DISCOUNTERS
BANKS AND BANKING-CHARTERED BANKS' REFUSAL TO CASH WELFARE CHEQUES. (B) EXISTENCE OF CHEQUE DISCOUNTERS
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I congratulate you on your memory. I also congratulate those who are stage managing the late show because we are able to have a debate on what I consider to be a very important topic. I rise on the same topic as that put forward by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), that is the disgraceful situation which is taking place in this country whereby low-income Canadians are being forced into the hands of loan sharks because the chartered banks in Canada are refusing to cash their cheques. These loan sharks charge horrendous rates of interest, rates which are way out of line and, I think, beyond the law. In any event, they are immoral, disgraceful and should not be allowed to continue. The banks are refusing to cash legitimate government cheques and those loan sharks are taking advantage of that particular situation.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg North mentioned tonight the latest instance of this, a case where the interest rate may be as high as 2,500 per cent, if one projects the rates on a daily basis. This must not be allowed to continue, Mr. Speaker.
I raised the subject on December 3 and I was very disappointed to hear the Parliamentary Secretary say tonight that it is still under consideration. It has been under consideration for almost a year now because this Party, when we were the Government, undertook through the previous Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to do something about this situation. Still we find that nothing has been done.
What can be done? First, the Minister of Finance could use moral suasion on the Canadian Bankers' Association in Toronto. He could say to the bankers that what has been going on in their banks must not be allowed to continue. They must be told that they must cash government cheques and must

January 29, 1985
Adjournment Debate
allow people on welfare and low-income Canadians who receive these cheques to get them cashed for nothing.
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) could also look at the law which came into being in Quebec in 1980. It states that no one can require fees from a consumer for cashing a cheque issued by the federal, provincial or municipal Governments. There have been some difficulties with that particular law in Quebec, but none, I feel, that cannot be overcome. Another possible solution, Mr. Speaker, is that government cheques could be directly deposited into people's accounts at the banks. In Great Britain there is another way of doing this whereby savings operations are attached to the Post Office and, therefore, anyone with a postal address has a savings account. Whatever course of action the Government chooses to take, this is a situation which cannot be allowed to continue.
The Parliamentary Secretary also said previously in answer that this situation arose quickly. Well, it has arisen over the past few years and that is hardly quickly. It is time now, I believe, for the Government to stop considering this matter and to take action so that these low-income Canadians can be treated fairly and justly as full Canadians in every sense of the word. The chartered banks of Canada are making good and healthy profits, Mr. Speaker, and it is not right, just or fair that these horrendous rates are charged to those who can least afford to pay that burden. It is a situation which should no longer continue to exist, and I call upon the Government, and upon the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to see that this situation is rectified right away.

speakeroldname: Mr. Claude Lanthier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING-CHARTERED BANKS' REFUSAL TO CASH WELFARE CHEQUES. (B) EXISTENCE OF CHEQUE DISCOUNTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no existing legislation compels
chartered banks to cash cheques issued by the Government of Canada. The only obligation of banks operating under the Bank Act is that they may not collect service charges for cashing Canadian Government cheques.
As a result of the ever-rising number of frauds, banks and other financial institutions are wary about cashing any kind of a cheque for non-clients. A few financial institutions do have mechanisms to help people who regularly receive payments from Governments or social agencies, but those mechanisms have not always given the expected results. Certain institutions have therefore specialized in cheque-cashing operations, but they may impose service charges since they do not come under the Bank Act.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) can understand why some of the financial institutions such as banks, trust companies and credit unions are hesitant to offer services to people who do not do business with them, and that is due to the prevalence of fraudulent transactions. However, he firmly believes that if the bearer of the cheque provides adequate identification and everything indicates that he or she is the legitimate owner of the cheque, then the financial institutions ought to honour the cheque, as they are required to do under their mandate.
The Minister will soon raise that important issue for poorer Canadians with spokesmen for banking institutions, and he will eventually recommend to the House or to the Government that appropriate steps be taken, as our colleague has just suggested, at least for moral if not legal considerations.
